docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• File names: lowercase, hyphens, no spaces (e.g., transformer-architecture.md)
  • Frontmatter: Every page must have YAML frontmatter (see below)
  • Wikilinks: Use [[page-name]] for internal links (Obsidian-style)
  • Internal page: [[page-name]]
  • Link to header: [[page-name#Header]]
  • Custom text: [[page-name|display text]]
  • External URL: [text](https://example.com/)
  • Minimum 2 outbound [wikilinks](hooks/wikilinks.py) per page
  • Citations: All pages derived from external material MUST cite sources
  • Frontmatter sources: field: list raw source files (e.g., sources: [raw/articles/source.md])
  • Inline provenance: ^[raw/articles/source.md] at paragraph level for specific claims
  • Readings and findings: MUST have sources (lint error if missing)
  • Concepts, entities, comparisons: SHOULD have sources when derived from material (lint warning)
  • Ideas: sources optional (original thoughts)
  • External URLs in prose should be captured to raw/ and cited, not left as bare links
  • Updates: Always bump updated date when modifying
  • Catalog: Add every new page to index-catalog.md
  • Log: Append every action to log.md
  • Raw sources: Never modify files in raw/ — they are immutable. Corrections go in wiki pages.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Every concept and entity must have a classification field in frontmatter
  2. Classification is a dot-path — e.g., classification: biotechnology.molecular-biology.dna-operations
  3. Minimum depth 2 — at least category.subcategory
  4. The tree is extensible — add new branches as content grows
  5. Review regularly — the lint script validates classifications against SCHEMA.md
  6. Sub-classifications can nest recursively — no depth limit

docs.title: Ideas
docs.text:
• Purpose: Raw thoughts, brainstorming, unprocessed notes
  • Threshold: No minimum - create for any thought worth keeping
  • Structure: Quick bullets, minimal structure
  • Example: "Idea for optimizing RAG retrieval with hierarchical clustering"

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• Purpose: Processed insights from research/analysis
  • Threshold: Create when processing reveals novel insight
  • Structure: Problem → Analysis → Conclusion → Sources
  • Example: "Video analysis revealed 3 key patterns in agent workflows"

docs.title: Readings
docs.text:
• Purpose: Summaries of books, papers, videos
  • Threshold: Create for every ingested source
  • Structure: Title, source, key points, quotes, related pages
  • Example: "LLM Wiki video notes with 5 key takeaways"

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
• Purpose: People, organizations, tools, projects
  • Threshold: Mentioned in 2+ sources OR central to 1 source
  • Structure: Overview, key facts, relationships, sources
  • Example: "Andrej Karpathy - AI researcher, former Tesla Autopilot director"

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Purpose: Technical concepts, theories, frameworks
  • Threshold: Explained in depth OR appears in 3+ sources
  • Structure: Definition, current state, open questions, related concepts
  • Example: "Transformer architecture - self-attention mechanism, multi-head attention, positional encoding"

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text:
• Purpose: Side-by-side analyses
  • Threshold: Whenever comparing 2+ items
  • Structure: What compared, dimensions, verdict, sources
  • Example: "Obsidian vs Notion vs Roam Research for knowledge management"

docs.title: Page Creation Rules
docs.text:
1. Ideas: No minimum threshold - create freely
  2. Readings: One per source - always create
  3. Entities: 2+ source mentions OR central to 1 source
  4. Concepts: Deep explanation OR 3+ source appearances
  5. Findings: Novel insight from processing
  6. Comparisons: When analyzing 2+ items

docs.title: Update Policy
docs.text: When new information conflicts with existing content: 1. Check dates - newer sources supersede older 2. If contradictory, note both with dates and sources 3. Mark in frontmatter: contradictions: [page-name] 4. Flag for user review during lint

docs.title: Quality Signals
docs.text:
• confidence: high (well-supported across sources), medium (some support), low (single source or opinion)
  • contested: true when unresolved contradictions exist
  • status: draft (new/unpolished), active (stable), archived (superseded)
  • reviewed: ISO date of last truth/validity check. Update after verifying page content against current sources. Lint flags pages not reviewed in 180 days, or updated after last review.

docs.title: Review Process
docs.text:
Periodically (at least every 6 months), review each active page: 1. Re-read the page and its cited sources 2. Check if information is still accurate / current 3. Check for contradictions with newer pages 4. Update content if needed, bump updated date 5. Set reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD (today's date) 6. If page is no longer accurate and can't be fixed → set status: archived

The lint script enforces this: - Active pages without reviewed → warning - Pages where updated > reviewed → warning (content changed since last review) - Pages not reviewed in 180+ days → info

docs.title: Copyright
docs.text: Raw source files in raw/ may contain copyrighted material. Rules: - Raw sources are for personal research use only — not redistributed via the public GitHub Pages site - The published wiki pages (concepts, entities, etc.) contain synthesis and quotes under fair use - When quoting, keep quotes short (<100 words) and always cite the source - If you receive a takedown request, remove the raw source immediately - Do not reproduce full articles — summarize and quote selectively

docs.title: Page Size
docs.text:
• Target: 50-150 lines per page
  • Split: When exceeding 200 lines
  • Archive: Move to _archive/ when fully superseded

Overall Health: ⚠️ Needs Attention — 205 warnings, 192 missing links, 20 orphan pages

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Neural Nexus has strong foundational structure — all required fields present, excellent classification coverage, functional graph connectivity. However, content migration from Hermes-Playground created significant technical debt: missing raw sources, undefined tags, broken wikilinks, orphan pages.

The wiki is functional but not production-ready for public deployment. With 15-25 hours of focused work addressing critical and high-priority issues, it can achieve excellent quality and be deployed confidently.

Strengths: - ✅ Solid schema compliance on core requirements - ✅ All pages properly classified - ✅ Functional knowledge graph (57 nodes, 96 edges) - ✅ Good content diversity (7 types, 3 domains)

Weaknesses: - ❌ Missing raw source files (citation integrity) - ❌ 35% of pages are orphans - ❌ 120+ broken wikilinks - ❌ 70+ undefined tags - ❌ Massive reference pages (navigation)

Opportunities: - Create findings from processed insights - Utilize ideas section for brainstorming - Improve link connectivity (192 suggestions available) - Expand into new domains (currently 3 active)

Threats: - Technical debt accumulation (migration issues) - Quality perception (warnings visible in lint) - Discoverability degradation (orphans, broken links)

docs.title: What's Compared
docs.text: This comparison examines the evolution of ADHD genetics research from early candidate gene studies to the latest genome-wide association meta-analysis, highlighting key methodological advances, discoveries, and clinical implications across different eras of research.

docs.title: Comparison Matrix
docs.text: Aspect Early Studies (1990s-2000s) Candidate Gene Era (2000s-2015) GWAS Era (2015-2020) Meta-Analysis Era (2020-Present) Sample Size Small (n < 1,000) Moderate (n = 1,000-5,000) Large (n = 5,000-20,000) Very Large (n = 70,000+) Methodology Candidate gene testing Candidate gene + GWAS early GWAS fine mapping Multi-cohort meta-analysis Loci Discovered Single genes Few loci (5-10) Moderate (10-20) Extensive (39 loci) Novel Genes Known biological candidates Some new discoveries Limited new genes 8 novel effector genes Statistical Power Low Moderate High Very High Effect Sizes Large ORs (2-5x) Moderate ORs (1.5-3x) Small ORs (1.1-1.5x) Very small ORs (1.01-1.1x) Biological Insights Limited Neurotransmission focus Pathway enrichment Comprehensive pathway mapping

docs.title: Early Studies (1990s-2000s)
docs.text:
Characteristics: - Candidate gene approach: Focused on genes with known biological relevance to ADHD - Small sample sizes: Limited statistical power - Family-based designs: TDT and linkage studies - Candidate genes: DRD2, DRD4, DAT1, 5-HTT, COMT

Key Findings: - Association with dopamine pathway genes - Limited replication across studies - Methodological limitations (population stratification) - Effect sizes typically large but inconsistent

Limitations: - Multiple testing: High false positive rates - Population bias: Primarily European ancestry - Small samples: Low power to detect true effects - Publication bias: Positive results favored

docs.title: Candidate Gene Era (2000s-2015)
docs.text:
Characteristics: - GWAS emergence: Transition from candidate to hypothesis-free approach - Moderate sample sizes: Improved statistical power - Genome-wide coverage: First true GWAS studies - Replication focus: Emphasis on independent replication

Key Studies: - Neale et al. (2010): First ADHD GWAS (n = 2,064) - Lasky-Su et al. (2012): Meta-analysis of multiple cohorts - Demontis et al. (2013): Large-scale GWAS

Key Findings: - Confirmation of dopamine pathway associations - Discovery of novel loci (e.g., CDH13) - Improved statistical methods - Better control for population structure

Advances: - Genome-wide coverage: Unbiased hypothesis testing - Improved statistics: Better control for false positives - Replication standards: Independent validation required - Meta-analysis methods: Initial multi-cohort approaches

docs.title: GWAS Era (2015-2020)
docs.text:
Characteristics: - Large sample sizes: Power to detect small effects - Advanced statistics: Fine mapping and polygenic risk scores - International consortia: Collaborative research networks - Functional annotation: Integration with biological data

Key Studies: - Demontis et al. (2019): 12 loci identified (20,183 cases, 35,191 controls) - Demontis et al. (2023): 27 loci identified (broader case definition) - Large-scale collaborations: Psychiatric Genomics Consortium ADHD working group

Key Findings: - 12-27 loci identified across studies - Polygenic risk scores: Clinical prediction potential - Biological pathways: Initial pathway enrichment - Genetic correlations: Comorbidity mapping

Methodological Advances: - Fine mapping: Identification of credible variant sets - Functional annotation: Integration with expression and epigenetic data - Cross-trait analysis: Genetic correlations with other disorders - Sex-stratified analysis: Investigation of sexual dimorphism

docs.title: Meta-Analysis Era (2020-Present)
docs.text:
Characteristics: - Very large samples: 70,000+ participants - Multi-cohort coordination: International research networks - Advanced statistics: Machine learning and causal inference - Comprehensive phenotyping: Symptom + diagnosis integration

Key Studies: - van der Laan et al. (2025): 39 loci (17 new), 70,953 participants - Combined phenotype approach: Symptoms + diagnosis integration - Advanced gene mapping: FLAMES and fine mapping

Key Findings: - 39 independent loci (17 newly discovered) - 8 novel effector genes with high confidence - Continuum model validation: Strong evidence for quantitative trait - Comprehensive pathway mapping: Synaptic and cell adhesion pathways - Improved polygenic scores: 2-3x improvement in prediction accuracy

Methodological Breakthroughs: - FLAMES analysis: Novel method for causal gene identification - Combined phenotype approach: Integration of quantitative and categorical measures - Multi-rater integration: Multiple assessment sources - Advanced statistics: Credible set identification and causal inference

docs.title: Loci Discovery Timeline
docs.text:
1990s-2000s: 0-5 loci (candidate gene era)
2000s-2015: 5-10 loci (early GWAS)
2015-2020: 10-27 loci (GWAS era)
2020-Present: 39 loci (meta-analysis era)

docs.title: Gene Discovery Progression
docs.text: Era Novel Genes Validation Level Early Known candidates Low Candidate Gene Some new discoveries Moderate GWAS Limited new genes High Meta-Analysis 8 novel effector genes Very High

docs.title: Effect Size Evolution
docs.text:
• Early studies: Large effects (OR 2-5x) but inconsistent
  • Candidate gene: Moderate effects (OR 1.5-3x) with better replication
  • GWAS: Small effects (OR 1.1-1.5x) with high confidence
  • Meta-analysis: Very small effects (OR 1.01-1.1x) but highly powered

docs.title: Pathway Discovery Progression
docs.text: Era Key Pathways Biological Understanding Early Dopamine neurotransmission Basic receptor function Candidate Gene Dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine Neurotransmitter systems GWAS Synaptic function, neuronal development Cellular and molecular mechanisms Meta-Analysis Synaptic density, cell adhesion, transcription Comprehensive biological networks

docs.title: Tissue-Specific Insights
docs.text:
• Early: Brain-wide associations
  • Candidate Gene: Region-specific hypotheses
  • GWAS: Tissue expression correlation
  • Meta-Analysis: Frontal cortex enrichment and cell-type specificity

docs.title: Risk Prediction Progression
docs.text: Era Prediction Accuracy Clinical Utility Early Poor (<5% variance) Limited Candidate Gene Moderate (5-10% variance) Limited GWAS Good (10-20% variance) Emerging Meta-Analysis Excellent (20-30% variance) Promising

docs.title: Diagnostic Applications
docs.text:
• Early: No clinical applications
  • Candidate Gene: Theoretical potential
  • GWAS: Research applications only
  • Meta-Analysis: Early clinical translation potential

docs.title: Treatment Implications
docs.text:
• Early: Symptomatic treatment focus
  • Candidate Gene: Medication response hypotheses
  • GWAS: Target identification
  • Meta-Analysis: Novel therapeutic targets (EMCN, PCDH17, etc.)

docs.title: Statistical Methods
docs.text:
• Early: Basic association tests
  • Candidate Gene: Multiple testing correction
  • GWAS: Genome-wide significance thresholds
  • Meta-Analysis: Advanced causal inference and fine mapping

docs.title: Sample Size Requirements
docs.text:
• Early: <1,000 participants
  • Candidate Gene: 1,000-5,000 participants
  • GWAS: 5,000-20,000 participants
  • Meta-Analysis: 70,000+ participants

docs.title: Quality Control
docs.text:
• Early: Basic quality control
  • Candidate Gene: Population structure control
  • GWAS: Advanced quality control and imputation
  • Meta-Analysis: Comprehensive quality control and harmonization

docs.title: Next Generation Research
docs.text:
1. Rare variants: Whole-genome sequencing for rare variant discovery
  2. Structural variants: Copy number variation and structural variant analysis
  3. Epigenetics: DNA methylation and histone modification studies
  4. Multi-omics integration: Proteomics, metabolomics, and transcriptomics

docs.title: Clinical Translation
docs.text:
1. Polygenic risk scores: Clinical implementation for early identification
  2. Pharmacogenomics: Treatment response prediction
  3. Personalized medicine: Individualized treatment approaches
  4. Prevention strategies: Early intervention for high-risk individuals

docs.title: Global Health Impact
docs.text:
1. Diverse populations: Expansion to non-European ancestry
  2. Health disparities: Addressing genetic and environmental inequities
  3. Global collaboration: International research networks
  4. Public health: Genetic burden assessment and resource allocation

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The evolution of ADHD genetics research demonstrates remarkable progress from early candidate gene studies to comprehensive meta-analyses. Key advances include:

  1. Sample size: From <1,000 to 70,000+ participants
  2. Discovery: From 0-5 loci to 39 loci with 8 novel effector genes
  3. Methodology: From basic tests to advanced causal inference
  4. Biological understanding: From neurotransmission to comprehensive pathway mapping
  5. Clinical translation: From theoretical to practical applications

The meta-analysis era, exemplified by van der Laan et al. (2025), represents a paradigm shift in ADHD genetics, providing unprecedented insights into the disorder's biological mechanisms and paving the way for improved diagnosis, treatment, and prevention strategies.

docs.title: China vs. Japan Economic Comparison
docs.text: Side-by-side analysis of structural economic challenges facing China and Japan, focusing on capital deepening, systemic differences, and recovery prospects.

docs.title: Capital Deepening: Core Metric Comparison
docs.text:
Aspect Japan (1990-2000) China (2008-2023) Comparison Capital-Output Ratio Increase +24% +62% China 2.5× Japan's rate Duration 10 years 15 years China's problem deeper Convergence Point N/A China ≈ Japan by 2022 China caught up to worst levels GDP Growth (current) ~1% (post-stagnation) Below 4.5-5% target Both below healthy levels Data Source Penn World Tables Penn World Tables Same methodology

Key Insight: China has accelerated capital deepening at 2.5× Japan's pace, reaching Japan's worst levels in just 15 years vs. Japan's 10-year lost decade^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md].

docs.title: Capital Source and Allocation
docs.text:
Dimension Japan (1990s) China (2008-2023) Impact Primary Source Borrowing/lending (QE, ultra-low rates) Export earnings, state policy direction Japan: Financial; China: Real economy Capital Flow Asset markets (real estate, stock speculation) Manufacturing, infrastructure, state-directed R&D Japan: Bubbles; China: Overproduction Motivation Corporate belief capital deepening = shareholder returns Policy fixation on "new quality productive forces" Japan: Market-driven; China: Policy-driven Market Context Post-bubble denial, stock market implosion Volatile equity markets, three sharp run-ups (2014-15, 2019-21, 2024-26) Japan: Crisis response; China: Continuous System Type Democratic, market economy Authoritarian, planned economy Japan: Market correction possible; China: Rigid

Key Difference: Japan's capital came from financial speculation (asset bubbles), while China's comes from actual export earnings re-leveraged into production^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md].

docs.title: Systemic Constraints: Democracy vs. Authoritarianism
docs.text:
Dimension Japan (Democratic) China (Authoritarian) Implications Policy Flexibility Can change course (elections, public pressure) Rigid top-down control Japan: Correction path exists; China: Locked in Public Welfare Cannot be cut (political suicide) Can be suppressed ("eat grass" theory) Japan: Consumption priority; China: Suppression possible Market Discipline Corporate accountability, bankruptcy exists State-owned enterprises, no failure allowed Japan: Failed companies exit; China: Zombie firms persist Consumption Priority Recognized as essential Suppressed by design Japan: Internal demand recovery possible; China: Blocked Recovery Mechanism Viable (internal demand + policy correction) Blocked by system design Japan: Path existed; China: Path blocked Political Accountability Elections force accountability Single-party rule, no accountability Japan: Policy errors corrected; China: Errors perpetuated

Critical Insight: Japan had the mechanism for recovery (democratic system) but failed to use it effectively. China's system is designed to prevent the very solution it needs (consumer-led rebalancing)^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md].

docs.title: Japan's Recovery Potential
docs.text:
What Japan Had: - Democratic system with elections - Government incentive to support citizens (they vote) - Market discipline mechanism (bankruptcy, accountability) - Ability to cut through denial with public pressure - Structural path to internal demand development

Why Japan Failed: - Policy errors: QE addiction, ultra-low interest rates - Asset market focus vs. real economy - Denial of structural problems - Lost time: 10 years → 30 years

Why Japan Eventually Recovered (Partially): - Democratic system allowed course correction - Consumer purchasing power preserved - Market mechanisms eventually cleared bad assets - Political accountability forced policy changes

docs.title: China's Recovery Obstacles
docs.text:
What China Lacks: - Democratic correction mechanism - Government incentive to support consumption - Market discipline (state-owned enterprises cannot fail) - Political accountability - Structural path to internal demand development

Why China Cannot Easily Recover: - Production-led model by design (not by accident) - Consumption suppression is policy choice, not constraint^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md] - State planning prevents market correction - Single-party rule locks in current trajectory - No mechanism to force policy changes

The "Worst of Both Systems" Problem: - Cannot successfully implement consumption suppression to sustainable level - Cannot transition to democratic system with consumption-led recovery - No viable path forward^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]

"The problem is we see China's economic situation: two systems' worst thing. It cannot make its people eat grass, but at the same time it cannot let people democratize."^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]

docs.title: Development Stage Comparison
docs.text:
Factor Japan (1990s) China (Current) Significance Wealth Level at Crisis Onset Already wealthy (per capita GDP ~$25,000) Not yet wealthy (per capita GDP ~$12,000) China: "未富先老" (getting old before getting rich)^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md] Demographics Aging population Rapid aging, more severe demographic pressure China's problem worse Urbanization Mostly complete Still in process China has more growth potential, but blocked by policy Debt Level High (corporate/government) Extremely high (local government, shadow banking) China's debt problem more complex External Dependencies Lower (domestic market strong) Extremely high (export-dependent) China more vulnerable to external shocks

Critical Difference: Japan got rich before experiencing structural decline. China is experiencing decline before reaching wealth levels^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]. This makes China's problem far more severe.

docs.title: Japan's Labor Cost Trajectory (1980s-1990s)
docs.text:
• Pre-crisis: Gradual wage increases as economy grew
  • Crisis onset (1990): Wage growth stagnated
  • Post-crisis: Wage compression due to deflation
  • Result: Labor costs fell, but demand collapsed alongside

docs.title: China's Labor Cost Trajectory (2000s-Present)
docs.text:
Period Event Impact on Capital-Output Ratio 2000-2007 Cheap labor, export boom Ratio declining (normal productivity gains) 2007-2014 Hu Jintao era: Labor law reforms, social protections Ratio rising (legitimate wage increases) 2014-Present Xi era: Failed capital allocation, R&D failures Ratio accelerating (capital misallocation)^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]

Key Distinction: China's early capital-output ratio rise (2007-2014) was legitimate (wage increases, labor protections). Post-2014 acceleration is structural (capital misallocation, failed investments).

docs.title: Japan: Asset Market Failures
docs.text:
• Real estate bubble: Land prices collapsed 80%+ from peak
  • Stock market bubble: Nikkei 225 fell from ~39,000 to ~7,000
  • Banking sector: Massive non-performing loans
  • Key feature: Failures were financial, not productive

docs.title: China: Productive Capital Failures
docs.text:
Project Investment Outcome Impact on Capital-Output Ratio Wuhan Hongxin Massive semiconductor investment Fraudulent EUV claim, completely failed Capital sunk, zero output^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md] Tsinghua Unigroup (紫光) State semiconductor fund investment Failed to compete Capital sunk, zero output AI data centers Post-2023 construction frenzy Low yield, high cost, overheating issues Capital rising faster than output^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md] High-end AI chips (DUV) Extremely expensive production method Low quality, reliability problems Capital rising faster than output

Critical Difference: China's failures are in productive capital, counted in the capital stock but generating no output. Japan's failures were in financial assets, which eventually cleared through market mechanisms.

docs.title: Japan's Techno-Optimism Trap (1980s)
docs.text:
Narrative: - Sony founder Akio Morita's books - Ezra Vogel's "Japan as Number One" - Clyde Prestowitz's "Trading Places" - Celebration of Japan's technological supremacy

Reality: - Technology success was real - Growth model was unsustainable - All missed the structural problem - Lesson: Technology ≠ sustainable growth^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md]

docs.title: China's Techno-Optimism Trap (2020s)
docs.text:
Narrative: - Evan Osnos's "The Future, Made in China" (The New Yorker, August 3, 2026) - Robots, "dark" factories, high-speed EVs, AI developments - Celebration of China's technological supremacy - Parallel to 1980s Japan hype^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md]

Reality: - Technology success is real - Growth model is unsustainable - Narrative accepts CCP's "hook, line, and sinker"^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md] - Same pattern, worse structural constraints

Roach's Critique:

"I was left wondering if he [Osnos] hasn't taken some of the CCP's bait too far — hook, line, and sinker... It's not that they under-estimated America — they all missed what was to befall Japan."^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md]

docs.title: Japan's Global Impact (1990s-Present)
docs.text:
• Limited: Primarily regional impact (Asia)
  • Financial contagion: Banking sector issues, but contained
  • Trade impact: Declining Japanese demand affected exports
  • Strategic lesson: Warning about asset bubbles, aging populations

docs.title: China's Global Impact (2000s-Present)
docs.text:
• Massive: Global economic impact
  • Inflation suppression: WTO entry kept global inflation low (2000s)^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]
  • Trade impact: Trillions in exports affecting every major economy
  • Strategic impact: China's model forces other countries to adjust

BYD Example: - Cheap Chinese EVs冲击 German auto market - Germany must cut welfare to compete - Race to bottom: China's production-only model forces global welfare suppression^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]

"Why do you talk about China? Because China is affecting the whole world. This is why China's case will definitely become more classic than Japan's lost 30 years."^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]

docs.title: Japan's Actual Outcome
docs.text:
• Lost decade × 3 (30 years of stagnation)
  • Partial recovery: Market mechanisms eventually cleared bad assets
  • Ongoing challenges: Aging population, deflationary pressures
  • System remains: Democratic mechanisms allow ongoing adjustment

docs.title: China's Potential Outcomes
docs.text:
Scenario Probability Description Likelihood Japan-style stagnation Low Demographic pressures, but stronger fundamentals Systemic differences make direct parallel unlikely Severe contraction Medium Production-led model collapse, external shocks hit thin margins More likely given margin compression vulnerability Protracted malaise High Current trajectory continues with incremental decline Most likely without structural change Systemic reform Very Low Transition to consumption-led model, democratic elements Blocked by system design Crisis-driven change Low-Medium External crisis forces structural adjustment Possible but unpredictable

Key Constraint: China's system is designed to prevent the very solution (consumer-led rebalancing) it needs^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]. Without systemic change, protracted malaise is most likely.

docs.title: Japan's Paradox
docs.text:
• Had the mechanism for recovery (democratic system)
  • Failed to use it effectively (policy errors, denial)
  • Eventually recovered partially after 3 lost decades
  • Lesson: Mechanisms exist, but must be used

docs.title: China's Paradox
docs.text:
• Doing what Japan did wrong (capital deepening)
  • With structural constraints Japan didn't face:
  • No democratic correction mechanism
  • No consumption recovery path
  • System designed to prevent the solution needed
  • Cannot escape the spiral Japan eventually navigated
  • Lesson: Structural constraints can be more damaging than policy errors

docs.title: Stephen Roach Analysis^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md]
docs.text:
• China's capital-output ratio up 62% (2.5× Japan's rate)
  • China has converged with Japan's worst levels by 2022
  • Capital deepening is policy-driven (Xi Jinping fixation), not market-driven
  • Current trajectory suggests intensification beyond 2023
  • Conclusion: China is deepening Japan's problems with worse constraints

docs.title: Podcast Analysis^[raw/transcripts/笑談中國經濟/stephen-roach-capital-deepening.md]
docs.text:
• Japan had democratic mechanisms, China doesn't
  • Japan got rich before stagnation, China hasn't
  • China gets "worst of both systems": No consumption + no recovery
  • China's global impact makes it more "classic" than Japan's case
  • Conclusion: Systemic constraints make China's problem fundamentally different and worse

docs.title: Michael Pettis Alignment
docs.text:
• Different frameworks, same bottom-line conclusion^[raw/pdfs/china-deepening-japan-problem-stephen-roach.md]
  • Japan's lesson: Problem wasn't technological success, but growth model sustainability
  • Same lesson applicable to China
  • Capital deepening is signal of Chinese growth model sputtering

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Capital Deepening Severity: China's capital-output ratio rose 2.5× faster than Japan's (62% vs. 24%)

  2. Systemic Constraints: Japan had recovery mechanisms; China's system blocks them

  3. Development Timing: Japan got rich before stagnation; China is declining before reaching wealth

  4. Capital Allocation: Japan's failures were financial; China's are productive (counted in capital stock, no output)

  5. Global Impact: Japan's impact was regional; China's is global

  6. Recovery Path: Japan had a viable path; China's is blocked by system design

  7. Technology Narrative: Both fell for techno-optimism trap; China's is worse due to structural constraints

  8. Core Problem: Same structural problem (capital deepening), but China's constraints are fundamentally different and more severe

docs.title: eMAG vs MagNA PURE 96 vs easyMAG Comparison
What's Being Compared
docs.text: Three nucleic acid extraction platforms for detection of common human respiratory viruses: - easyMAG (bioMérieux) - Semi-automated, 24 samples - eMAG (bioMérieux) - Fully automated, 48 samples - MagNA PURE 96 (Roche) - Fully automated, 96 samples

docs.title: Why Compare
docs.text:
Clinical laboratories need to select extraction platforms based on: - Sample volume and throughput requirements - Available laboratory space - Automation preferences - Operational complexity - Cost considerations - Performance characteristics (sensitivity, specificity, LOD)

This comparison provides evidence-based guidance for platform selection using data from a comprehensive validation study of 262 respiratory samples across 6 viruses.^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

docs.title: Comparison Matrix
docs.text: Dimension easyMAG eMAG MagNA PURE 96 Manufacturer bioMérieux (France) bioMérieux (France) Roche (Germany) Automation Semi-automated Fully automated Fully automated Capacity 24 samples 48 samples 96 samples Extraction Time ~60 min ~90 min ~90 min Technology Silica (BOOM) Silica (BOOM) Magnetic beads Dimensions 100×65×53 cm 142×80×181 cm 136×81.5×100 cm Sample Loading Manual to cartridge Direct from tube Robotic loader required Barcode Reader Manual Built-in Manual Nucleic Acid Collection Cartridge → manual transfer Direct to tubes Plate → robotic transfer User Convenience Very easy Complex (dual subunits) Very easy Lab Size Fit Small Medium Large Launch Year 2005 ~2018 2009

docs.title: Analytical Sensitivity
docs.text:
Platform Overall Sensitivity Overall Specificity PPV NPV easyMAG 99.4% 99.3% 97.7% 99.3% eMAG >99% >98% 97.7% 99.8% MagNA PURE 96 97.7% 99.5% 98.3% 99.3%

Conclusion: All platforms demonstrate excellent clinical performance (>97% sensitivity, >98% specificity). Performance differences are negligible for clinical decision-making.

docs.title: Inter-platform Agreement
docs.text:
Metric Value Kappa coefficient >0.973 (excellent agreement)^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md] Ct value SD <1.0 across all platforms (excellent correlation)^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md] Bland-Altman agreement >98% of samples within 2 SD boundaries^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md] Sample type agreement >97% across BAL, tracheal aspirations, nasopharyngeal swabs^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

Conclusion: Platforms produce highly consistent results. Choice should not be based on performance differences.

docs.title: Limit of Detection Comparison
docs.text:
Virus easyMAG eMAG MagNA PURE 96 Stock Source Influenza A 10⁻² 10⁻³ 10⁻³ WHO Influenza B 10⁻³ 10⁻³ 10⁻³ WHO H1N1pdm 10⁻⁴ 10⁻⁴ 10⁻⁴ WHO Adenovirus 10⁻⁵ 10⁻⁵ 10⁻⁵ ATCC RSV 10⁻⁶ 10⁻⁵ 10⁻⁵ ATCC Parainfluenza-3 10⁻⁵ 10⁻⁵ 10⁻⁵ Clinical hMPV 10⁻³ 10⁻⁴ 10⁻³ Clinical

Conclusion: LOD differences are within one dilution factor. High dilution samples have very low virus concentrations and are mostly undetected according to Poisson distribution. These differences are clinically negligible.^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

docs.title: easyMAG Advantages
docs.text:
✅ Fastest extraction time (~60 min) - enables rapid turnaround for urgent samples^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Smallest footprint (100×65×53 cm) - suitable for space-constrained laboratories^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Very easy to operate - minimal training required^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Established platform - extensively validated since 2005^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Proven performance - extensive literature validation for various clinical applications^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

❌ Limited capacity (24 samples) - requires multiple runs for high-volume labs

❌ Semi-automated - requires manual cartridge loading and transfer

❌ Manual barcode reader - no built-in scanning capability

docs.title: eMAG Advantages
docs.text:
✅ Balanced capacity (48 samples) - suitable for medium-sized laboratories^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Built-in barcode reader - enables simple load-and-run workflow with barcoded tubes^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Direct sample loading - extract from primary tubes (1.5-14 mL)^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Direct to collection tubes - no manual transfer needed^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Dual subunit design - flexible for ≤24 sample runs (run one subunit, leave the other idle)^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Same technology as easyMAG - BOOM silica-based extraction with proven performance^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

❌ Complex operation (dual 24-sample subunits) - confusing sample loading without barcodes^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

❌ Largest footprint (142×80×181 cm) - requires significant laboratory space

❌ Longer extraction time (~90 min) - slower than easyMAG

❌ Requires well-trained technician for proper operation^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

docs.title: MagNA PURE 96 Advantages
docs.text:
✅ Highest throughput (96 samples) - suitable for high-volume laboratories^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Very easy to operate - user-friendly linear loading in 16-sample racks^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Proven performance - excellent nucleic acid extraction efficiency for clinical samples^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Magnetic bead technology - scalable to 96-well plate format^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

✅ Middle footprint (136×81.5×100 cm) - between easyMAG and eMAG

❌ Requires robotic loader - additional equipment needed for sample loading^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

❌ Extra transfer steps - nucleic acids to plate, then robotic transfer to PCR plates or tubes^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

❌ Manual barcode reader - no built-in scanning capability

❌ Large infrastructure requirement - suitable only for laboratories with existing automation

docs.title: High-Volume Laboratories (>50 samples/run)
docs.text:
Recommendation: MagNA PURE 96

Rationale: - Maximum throughput (96 samples) meets volume requirements - User-friendly operation reduces technician time - Proven performance in high-volume settings - Integration with 96-well plate workflows

When to choose despite cons: - Laboratory has robotic infrastructure - Sample volume justifies investment in robotic loader - Workflow is plate-based (PCR setup, result reporting)

docs.title: Medium-Sized Laboratories (25-50 samples/run)
docs.text:
Recommendation: eMAG

Rationale: - Balanced capacity (48 samples) matches typical volume - Built-in barcode reader enables simple workflow - Direct tube-to-tube extraction reduces manual steps - Dual subunit design provides flexibility for smaller runs

When to choose despite cons: - Laboratory uses barcoded sample tubes - Technicians are well-trained on dual subunit operation - Space is available for larger footprint - Value balanced automation over fastest turnaround

docs.title: Low-Volume Laboratories (<25 samples/run)
docs.text:
Recommendation: easyMAG

Rationale: - Fastest turnaround (~60 min) enables rapid reporting - Smallest footprint fits space-constrained labs - Very easy to operate with minimal training - Established reliability and extensive validation

When to choose despite cons: - Sample volume rarely exceeds 24 samples - Urgent testing requires rapid turnaround - Laboratory space is limited - Technical staff have minimal automation experience

docs.title: Sample Type Considerations
docs.text:
All platforms demonstrated >97% agreement across sample types:^[raw/laboratory/validation/emag-magana-easymag-respiratory-virus-extraction-comparison.md]

  • Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Viscous samples required dilution with M199 transport media for all platforms
  • Tracheal aspirations: Viscous samples required dilution with M199 transport media for all platforms
  • Nasopharyngeal swabs: No special processing required

Conclusion: Sample type performance is equivalent across platforms. No platform has advantage for specific sample types.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Adaptive sampling is a dynamic data collection methodology that uses real-time analysis and decision-making to optimize resource allocation and data quality during experimental processes. Unlike static sampling strategies, adaptive approaches continuously evaluate incoming data and adjust collection parameters based on predefined criteria, scientific objectives, and emerging patterns, resulting in more efficient and effective data acquisition.

docs.title: Core Mechanism
docs.text:
The fundamental principle of adaptive sampling involves:

  1. Real-time Monitoring: Continuous evaluation of incoming data quality and content
  2. Decision Analysis: Algorithmic assessment of sampling effectiveness and objectives
  3. Dynamic Adjustment: Modification of collection parameters based on evaluation
  4. Quality Control: Integration of quality assessment throughout the process

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Adaptive sampling is crucial because: - Resource Optimization: Maximizes data quality while minimizing resource consumption - Scientific Efficiency: Accelerates discovery through intelligent data collection - Enhanced Accuracy: Reduces noise and focuses on high-value data - Flexibility: Adapts to unexpected findings and changing objectives - Cost-Effectiveness: Reduces experimental time and resource requirements - Improved Reproducibility: Consistent sampling strategies across experiments

docs.title: ADHD Risk Genes and Effect Sizes
Overview
docs.text: This page compiles the complete list of genes associated with increased risk of ADHD based on the largest genome-wide association meta-analysis to date (van der Laan et al., 2025). The analysis identified 39 independent loci and 22 potential ADHD effector genes, with comprehensive effect size data and biological function annotations.

docs.title: Effect Size Interpretation
docs.text:
• Odd Ratios (OR): Not directly provided in the GWAS meta-analysis
  • Effect Size: Primarily measured as beta coefficients from association tests
  • FLAMES Score: Confidence score for causal effector genes (higher = more confident)
  • Genetic Risk: Expressed as variance explained by polygenic scores (0.3-3.1%)

docs.title: Study Design Impact
docs.text:
• Sample Size: 70,953 individuals with 290,134 ADHD measures
  • Combined Analysis: ADHD symptoms + diagnosis data (improved power)
  • Discovery vs. Replication: 17 new loci discovered, 22 previously known
  • Statistical Power: High power to detect small effect sizes due to large sample

docs.text:

Key Features of Novel Genes: - All 8 genes have FLAMES scores > 0.08, indicating high confidence in causal role - Multiple genes involved in cell adhesion (EMCN, PCDH17, CTNNA2) - Kinase activity represented (STK32C, PEAK1) - Growth factor signaling (IGF1R) - Novel transcriptional regulation (TCF12)

docs.title: Polygenic Risk Score Performance
docs.text:
The study tested three polygenic risk score approaches across three independent cohorts:

Polygenic Score Variance Explained Performance Rank Cohorts Tested ADHDOVERALL (Combined) 0.3-3.1% Best ALSPAC, MoBa, NTR ADHDDIAG (Diagnosis only) 0.2-2.5% Moderate ALSPAC, MoBa, NTR ADHDSYMP (Symptoms only) 0.1-1.2% Lowest ALSPAC, MoBa, NTR

Key Finding: Combining ADHD symptoms with diagnosis data improves prediction accuracy by 2-3x.

docs.title: Individual Variant Effects
docs.text: While individual SNP effects are small (typical for complex traits), the combined effect is substantial: - SNP heritability: h²SNP = 0.11 (11% of variance explained by common variants) - Total heritability: Estimated 70-80% heritability for ADHD - Missing heritability: Large portion likely due to rare variants and structural variants

docs.text: Genes are enriched in: - Frontal cortex: Key region for executive function and attention - Striatum: Involved in reward processing and motor control - Hippocampus: Memory and learning - Cerebellum: Motor coordination and cognitive processing

docs.title: Risk Prediction
docs.text:
• Polygenic Risk Scores: Can explain 0.3-3.1% of variance in ADHD risk
  • Clinical Utility: Best when combined with symptom assessment and family history
  • Population Screening: May identify high-risk children for early intervention

docs.title: Treatment Implications
docs.text:
• Pharmacogenomics: Genes involved in neurotransmission (DRD5) may predict medication response
  • Novel Targets: Cell adhesion genes (CDH13, PCDH17) suggest new therapeutic approaches
  • Pathway-Specific Treatments: Synaptic pathway enrichment supports neurodevelopmental treatments

docs.title: Developmental Considerations
docs.text:
• Age-Specific Effects: Some genes may have different effects across developmental stages
  • Gene-Environment Interactions: Environmental factors may modify genetic risk
  • Epigenetic Regulation: Environmental influences on gene expression

docs.title: Study Limitations
docs.text:
1. Population Bias: Primarily European ancestry limits generalizability
  2. Age Focus: Childhood-focused; adult ADHD less represented
  3. Effect Size Magnitude: Individual SNP effects are small (OR typically 1.01-1.05)
  4. Missing Heritability: Large portion of heritability not explained by common variants

docs.title: Interpretation Challenges
docs.text:
1. Correlation vs. Causation: Genetic correlations don't imply causal relationships
  2. Pleiotropy: Genes affect multiple traits, making specific attribution difficult
  3. Population Stratification: Despite QC, some residual population structure may exist

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition spanning cognitive, behavioral, and affective domains: (a) attentional processing and executive function, (b) response inhibition and impulsive behavior, and (c) overactive motor output. Diagnosis is made when these symptoms lie at the far end of the normative continuum and yield impairment in essential life functions.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

Like nearly all forms of psychopathology, the constituent behaviors are spectrum-related phenomena; dimensional accounts are usually superior to categorical models with respect to scientific validity.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Executive Function Deficits
docs.text: The most replicated cognitive finding in ADHD is impaired executive function (EF) — including response inhibition, working memory, planning, and cognitive flexibility.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md] EF deficits are neither necessary nor sufficient for all cases, but they constitute a core pathway.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Multiple Neural Pathways
docs.text:
ADHD is not a single-deficit disorder. Multiple partially independent mechanisms contribute:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

Mechanism Description Executive dysfunction Inhibition, working memory, planning deficits Delay aversion Preference for immediate over delayed rewards Reaction time variability Inconsistent response speed (319+ studies meta-analyzed) Reward pathway dysfunction Dopamine reward pathway anomalies (Volkow et al. 2009, 2010) Default mode network Intrusion of task-negative networks during focused activity Cortical maturation delay Delayed cortical thinning, particularly prefrontal cortex (Shaw et al. 2007)

These multiple pathways produce equifinality — different causal forces converging on parallel symptom displays — and multifinality — early markers not inevitably associated with later impairment.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Heritability
docs.text:
ADHD is among the most heritable psychiatric conditions:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

Population Heritability Symptom dimensions (youth) ~0.75 Clinically diagnosed cases ~0.90 Adults (self-report) Appears lower Adults (cross-informant/clinical) Nearly as high as youth

Key caveats:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md] - High heritability does NOT mean single genes are responsible — combinations of many genes act in concert - High heritability does NOT mean environments lack importance - Shared genetic vulnerability exists across major psychiatric disorders (Cross-Disorder Group 2013) - Heritabilities may not be uniform across socioeconomic spectra

docs.title: Risk Factors
docs.text: Factor Evidence Low birth weight Lower weight → higher ADHD risk; dose-response relationship Prenatal alcohol Binges → fetal alcohol syndrome; lesser amounts → ADHD symptoms Prenatal nicotine Complex gene × toxic interaction (Thapar et al. 2009) Lead exposure Implicated in ADHD symptoms and compromised IQ Severe early deprivation Romanian adoptee studies show ADHD-like patterns Organophosphate pesticides CHAMACOS study: exposure linked to attention problems Prenatal acetaminophen Long-term exposure linked to differential gene methylation in ADHD

docs.title: Gene–Environment Interplay
docs.text: ADHD is expressed via transactional patterns involving:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md] - Gene–environment correlation (rGE): genetic propensities shape the environments individuals experience - Gene–environment interaction (G×E): genetic liability is potentiated by environmental factors - Epigenetic forces: environmental exposures alter gene expression patterns (e.g., Gervin et al. 2017)

docs.title: Onset and Persistence
docs.text:
• Symptoms often emerge during preschool years^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]
  • More often than not, ADHD extends into adulthood^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]
  • Longitudinal studies (Klein et al. 2012) show continuing impairment 33 years after childhood diagnosis^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Comorbidity
docs.text:
ADHD shows high comorbidity with:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

Domain Conditions Externalizing ODD, conduct disorder, substance use Internalizing Anxiety, depression Learning Dyslexia, specific learning disorders Neurodevelopmental Autism spectrum, language disorders

Comorbidity patterns differ by gender: boys show more externalizing comorbidities; girls show more internalizing.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Life-Span Impairments
docs.text:
Life Stage Impairments Childhood Academic underachievement, social rejection, accidental injury Adolescence Delinquency, substance use, risky behavior, peer problems Adulthood Unemployment, substance abuse, risky driving, self-harm, relationship problems

US costs: hundreds of billions of dollars annually (direct + indirect).^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Girls and Women with ADHD
docs.text:
Females are chronically underdiagnosed and understudied:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

Aspect Finding Referral bias Boys 3–4× more likely to be referred for treatment Symptom presentation Girls show more inattentive, fewer hyperactive symptoms Comorbidity More internalizing, eating pathology, self-harm Adult outcomes Elevated risk for suicide attempts, intimate partner victimization Parenting stress Mediates outcomes for girls with ADHD

Key prospective studies (Hinshaw et al. 2002, 2006, 2012; Owens et al. 2017) follow girls with ADHD into early adulthood, showing continuing cross-domain impairment and elevated risk for self-injury and suicide attempts.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Surging US Prevalence
docs.text:
US diagnosed prevalence has risen 41% in the past decade; 11% of youth aged 4–17 now diagnosed.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md] Contributing factors:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

Factor Mechanism Increased recognition Greater awareness among clinicians and parents Policy changes ADHD diagnosis → eligibility for services NCLB accountability Unintended consequence: ADHD diagnoses increase in low-SES public schools Pharmaceutical advertising US + New Zealand only nations allowing direct-to-consumer drug ads Geographic variation Mirrors "small area variation" in healthcare (Wennberg & Gittelsohn 1973)

Worldwide prevalence is consistently ~5–7% across nations with compulsory education, suggesting the underlying symptom domains reflect a neurobiological propensity that emerges in classroom settings.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text: Myth Reality ADHD is a US-only phenomenon Worldwide prevalence ~5–7%; exists across cultures ADHD is just fidgety boys Affects females, adults, all socioeconomic groups ADHD is caused by bad parenting Highly heritable (~0.75); parenting interacts with but doesn't cause ADHD ADHD is overdiagnosed everywhere US diagnosed prevalence outstrips true prevalence, but many cases are also missed (especially girls) Stimulants are "smart pills" Cognitive enhancement in healthy people is modest and inconsistent ADHD is outgrown Often persists into adulthood with different symptom presentation All-biological or all-cultural Reductionist — both interact transactionally Medication alone is sufficient Multimodal treatment needed for functional outcomes

docs.title: Evidence-Based Interventions
docs.text: Treatment Evidence Target Stimulant medication 70–80% acute response rate; first-line Core symptom reduction Behavioral parent training Strong evidence; meta-analysis (Fabiano et al. 2009) Parenting practices, home behavior Classroom management Strong evidence Academic functioning, school behavior CBT for adult ADHD Evidence-based (Solanto 2011) Executive dysfunction, coping skills Multimodal (med + behavioral) MTA study: optimal for promoting competencies Functional outcomes

docs.title: MTA Study
docs.text: The Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD (MTA) is the landmark longitudinal RCT. Key findings:^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md] - 14-month trial: carefully monitored medication + behavioral intervention superior for promoting competencies - Long-term follow-up (8+ years): initial benefits diminish without continued treatment - Medication alone insufficient for functional outcomes (academic, social, emotional) - Adolescent substance use related more to childhood conduct than to medication exposure

docs.title: Insufficient Evidence
docs.text: Treatment Status Neurofeedback Triple-blind RCT showed no superiority over sham (Schönenberg et al. 2017) Working memory training Limited transfer; gains don't generalize to ADHD symptoms Physical exercise Promising but preliminary Dietary restrictions Meta-analysis shows small effects for food color additives in subset

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
1. Specific genes contributing to ADHD vulnerability remain elusive^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]
  2. Gene–environment interplays relevant to particular symptoms and impairments largely unknown^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]
  3. Heterogeneity in symptom presentations, mechanisms, and outcomes needs untangling^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]
  4. Manifestations in females and adults remain less well identified^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]
  5. Precision intervention — matching treatments to individual profiles — urgently needed^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: ADHD is one of the most prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions worldwide, with massive personal, familial, and economic costs. Understanding it requires multiple levels of analysis — spanning genes, neurotransmission, brain pathways, individual skill levels, family socialization, peer relationships, and educational and cultural forces — which must be integrated to surpass reductionist accounts, reduce stigma, and maximize the impact of prevention and intervention efforts.^[raw/articles/hinshaw-2018-adhd-review.md]

docs.title: First-Line Medications
docs.text: Stimulant medications constitute the first-line treatment for ADHD, with response rates of 70-80% for acute symptom reduction. Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine dimesylate) is a Schedule II controlled substance and CNS stimulant that acts as a prodrug, converting to dextroamphetamine to increase dopamine and norepinephrine neurotransmission.

docs.title: Key Medication Characteristics
docs.text: Medication Class Mechanism Duration Abuse Potential Vyvanse Amphetamine prodrug Dopamine/norepinephrine release 10-14 hours High (CII) Other stimulants Various Similar mechanisms Variable High (CII)

docs.title: MTA Study Findings
docs.text: The landmark Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD (MTA) demonstrated: - 14-month trial: Carefully monitored medication + behavioral intervention superior for promoting competencies - Long-term follow-up: Initial benefits diminish without continued treatment - Medication alone insufficient for functional outcomes (academic, social, emotional)

docs.title: 預設醫療指示的法律程序和實施
Overview
docs.text: 預設醫療指示的法律程序和實施是一個複雜但重要的過程，涉及法律、醫療和倫理多個層面。這個過程確保患者在失去決策能力時，其醫療意願能夠得到尊重和執行。本頁面將詳細分析預設醫療指示的完整法律程序，從制定到實施的每個環節。

docs.title: 第一階段：資格評估和能力確認
患者資格確認
docs.text:
法律要求： - 年齡要求：必須年滿18歲 - 心智能力：必須具有精神行為能力 - 理解能力：必須理解醫療決定的後果 - 自願性：必須是自願作出決定

能力評估程序： 1. 醫生評估：由註冊醫生進行正式的能力評估 2. 心理測試：使用標準化工具評認知功能 3. 理解測試：測試對醫療信息的理解程度 4. 決定能力：評估作出醫療決定的能力

docs.title: 能力評估標準
docs.text:
認知能力： - 記憶力：能夠記住醫療信息 - 理解力：能夠理解醫療選項和後果 - 判斷力：能夠作出合理的醫療決定 - 溝通能力：能夠清楚表達自己的意願

法律能力： - 法律意識：理解決定的法律後果 - 預見能力：能預見決定的長期影響 - 自主能力：能夠獨立作出決定 - 責任能力：能夠承擔決定的責任

docs.title: 第二階段：信息提供和討論
醫療信息提供
docs.text:
信息內容： - 病情信息：當前醫療狀況和預後 - 治療選項：所有可行的治療選項 - 風險效益：各選項的風險和效益 - 替代方案：不治療或舒緩治療的選項

信息呈現方式： - 口頭解釋：醫生口頭詳細解釋 - 書面資料：提供書面的醫療資料 - 視覺輔助：使用圖表和視覺輔助工具 - 時間安排：給予足夠時間考慮和提問

docs.title: 決定討論
docs.text:
討議內容： - 價值觀探討：患者的價值觀和生活偏好 - 生活目標：患者的生活目標和期望 - 治療偏好：對不同治療方式的偏好 - 終末期考量：對終末期照護的看法

溝通技巧： - 傾聽技巧：積極傾聽患者的意見 - 提問技巧：使用開放式問題深入了解 - 同理心：展示對患者情感的理解 - 尊重態度：尊重患者的決定權

docs.title: 第三階段：文件制定和簽署
文件內容要求
docs.text:
法律文件： - 標準表格：使用政府制定的标准表格 - 內容完整：包含所有必要的法律要素 - 語言清晰：使用清晰易懂的語言 - 格式標準：符合法律文件的格式要求

具體內容： - 個人信息：患者的個人識別信息 - 醫療狀況：當前的醫療狀況描述 - 治療偏好：具體的治療偏好和限制 - 生效條件：指示生效的具體條件 - 見證人信息：見證人的身份信息 - 簽署日期：文件簽署的日期

docs.title: 簽署程序
docs.text:
見證人要求： - 見證人數量：需要兩名見證人 - 醫生見證：其中一名必須是註冊醫生 - 獨立性：見證人必須與患者無利益衝突 - 能力要求：見證人必須有能力理解文件內容

簽署程序： 1. 文件確認：見證人確認文件內容 2. 身份核實：核實見證人身份 3. 簽署見證：見證人在文件上簽署 4. 日期記錄：記錄簽署日期和時間 5. 文件保存：保存簽署完成的文件

docs.title: 第四階段：文件保存和管理

docs.title: 結論
docs.text:
預設醫療指示的法律程序和實施是一個複雜但重要的過程，涉及法律、醫療和倫理多個層面。通過完整的法律程序、嚴格的實施標準、有效的監督機制和充分的溝通協調，確保患者在失去決策能力時，其醫療意願能夠得到尊重和執行。

未來，隨著社會的變化和醫療技術的發展，這個法律程序需要不斷完善，以更好地服務社會需求和保障患者權益。同時，公眾教育和專業培訓也是未來發展的重要方向，確保這個法律程序能夠得到有效實施。

docs.title: 預設醫療指示與不作心肺復甦命令
Overview
docs.text: This concept covers the legal framework for advance medical directives in Hong Kong, focusing on advance medical directives (預設醫療指示) and do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation orders (不作心肺復甦命令). These legal instruments allow individuals to specify their medical treatment preferences when they lose decision-making capacity, protecting patient autonomy and preventing family conflicts during medical emergencies.

docs.title: Advance Medical Directives (預設醫療指示)
docs.text:
Advance medical directives are legal documents that allow competent adults to specify their wishes regarding life-sustaining treatment when they lose capacity.

Legal Requirements: - Must be 18+ years old with mental capacity - Must understand the consequences of refusing treatment - Requires two witnesses, one being a registered doctor - Must be written when the person has decision-making capacity

Scope: - Specifies preferences for life-sustaining treatment - Applies when person loses mental capacity - Cannot include requests for euthanasia or assisted death - Ensures natural death process with basic care and palliative treatment

docs.title: Do Not Attempt Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Orders (不作心肺復甦命令)
docs.text:
DNACPR orders are medical orders issued by doctors when resuscitation would be harmful or against the patient's best interests.

Medical Process: - Issued by two registered doctors jointly - Based on professional medical judgment - Applied when resuscitation would be harmful or futile - Cannot be issued against the patient's previously expressed wishes

For Incapacitated Patients: - Doctors must consult with responsible persons (family, guardians) - If no responsible person found, doctors consider patient's past wishes and values - Design protects medical decision-making professionalism while respecting family rights

docs.title: Hong Kong Legal Basis
docs.text:
The legal framework is established under the Medical Treatment (End of Life) Ordinance, which provides:

  1. Patient Autonomy: Right to make decisions about one's own medical care
  2. Medical Decision-Making: Clear processes for incapacitated patients
  3. Family Protection: Prevents families from feeling decisions were made secretly
  4. Professional Standards: Ensures medical decisions follow professional guidelines

docs.title: Key Legal Distinctions
docs.text:
Advance Directives vs Euthanasia: - Advance directives allow refusal of treatment but not active killing - Cannot request "please give me euthanasia" or "don't give me water" - Focuses on allowing natural death process with appropriate care - Euthanasia and medical assistance in dying remain illegal in Hong Kong

Medical Decision-Making Process: - For competent patients: Direct personal choice via advance directives - For incompetent patients: Doctor consultation with responsible persons - Fallback mechanism: Based on patient's previously expressed wishes and values

docs.title: Emergency Situations
docs.text:
When patients suddenly lose consciousness (e.g., from accidents, medical emergencies):

  1. Without Planning: Families face difficult decisions, potential conflicts
  2. With Advance Directives: Clear guidance reduces family stress and suffering
  3. Medical Response: Doctors follow documented wishes rather than defaulting to aggressive treatment

docs.title: Patient Scenarios
docs.text:
Terminal Cancer Patients: - May specify preferences for comfort over aggressive treatment - Can avoid painful resuscitation procedures - Ensure dignified death process

Elderly Patients: - Prevent unnecessary suffering from aggressive interventions - Allow natural death with appropriate palliative care - Reduce family burden during difficult times

Emergency Situations: - Sudden loss of consciousness from accidents - Medical emergencies where quick decisions are needed - Prevents "default" aggressive treatment that may cause harm

docs.title: Patient Rights
docs.text:
• Autonomy: Right to control medical treatment decisions
  • Dignity: Right to die with dignity without unnecessary suffering
  • Informed Consent: Must understand consequences of treatment decisions
  • Privacy: Medical decisions remain confidential until needed

docs.title: Family Considerations
docs.text:
• Reduced Burden: Families don't have to make difficult decisions under stress
  • Conflict Prevention: Prevents family disputes about treatment preferences
  • Emotional Protection: Reduces guilt and stress during medical emergencies

docs.title: Medical Professional Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Professional Judgment: Must act in patient's best interests
  • Communication: Must explain rationale clearly to families
  • Documentation: Proper procedures and witness requirements
  • Ethical Practice: Balance patient wishes with medical ethics

docs.title: Creating Advance Medical Directives
docs.text:
1. Assessment: Confirm mental capacity and understanding
  2. Discussion: Explain treatment options and consequences
  3. Documentation: Write clear, specific preferences
  4. Witnessing: Two witnesses required (one registered doctor)
  5. Storage: Keep document accessible to medical providers
  6. Review: Periodically review and update as needed

docs.title: Medical Order Process for DNACPR
docs.text:
1. Medical Assessment: Determine if resuscitation would be harmful or futile
  2. Professional Consultation: Joint decision by two registered doctors
  3. Family Consultation: Discuss with responsible persons if available
  4. Documentation: Complete proper medical order forms
  5. Implementation: Ensure all medical staff aware of the order
  6. Review: Regularly reassess patient condition

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Amyloid-beta (Aβ) is a peptide derived from amyloid precursor protein (APP) that aggregates into insoluble plaques in the brain, serving as the primary constituent of neuritic plaques in and other neurodegenerative diseases.^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Production and Regulation
docs.text:
• Cleaved from APP sequentially by β-secretase (BACE1) and γ-secretase^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • Released from neurons in a manner modulated by synaptic activity^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • Regulated by SORL1 (sortilin-related receptor-1), a neuronal receptor that controls APP trafficking to decrease Aβ conversion^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • Loss-of-function SORL1 mutations are important genetic risk factors for AD^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Aggregation Pathway
docs.text:
Aβ monomers (particularly Aβ42, which is more aggregation-prone) self-aggregate through intermediate stages: 1. Oligomers: Small soluble aggregates 2. Protofibrils: Intermediate species (pathogenic; targeted by lecanemab) 3. Mature fibrils: Insoluble cross-β-pleated sheet structures 4. Amyloid plaques: Deposits in brain tissue

As plaques age, Aβ undergoes post-translational modifications: - N-terminal pyroglutamate modification (pE3-Aβ; pathogenic; targeted by donanemab) - Phosphorylation (pSer8Aβ)^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• Aβ accumulation begins in brain ~20 years before cognitive impairment onset^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • Considered a critical first step in AD pathological cascade
  • However, cognitive decline correlates more strongly with tau-pathology than amyloid burden^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Cryo-EM Insights
docs.text: studies revealed disease-specific Aβ conformations with important implications: - Sporadic AD Aβ42 filaments differ from familial AD filaments^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Both differ from Aβ40 filament structures^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Down syndrome-associated AD (DSAD) shows both shared and novel filaments^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Critical finding: Brain-derived filaments differ markedly from synthetically derived fibrils in side-chain orientations, contacts, and packing^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Disease Modeling Implications
docs.text:
• Synthetic fibrils may not accurately model human disease^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • AppNL-F knockin mouse Aβ42 filaments match human brain-derived filaments from DIAD (but caution in extrapolating to sporadic AD)^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Clinical Trial Evidence
docs.text:
Therapeutic successes identify which Aβ species are most pathogenic:

Aβ Species Therapeutic Target Clinical Outcome Evidence Protofibrils Lecanemab ~30% slowing cognitive decline over 18 months CLARITY-AD trial^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] pE3-Aβ plaques Donanemab Similar slowing of decline TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] Monomers Solanezumab Failed to show benefit No clinical improvement^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] Fibrils Aducanumab Equivocal outcomes Inconclusive evidence^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Mechanism of Action
docs.text: Anti-Aβ antibodies clear plaques via Fc-mediated microglial activation and phagocytosis^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - This explains why crenezumab (IgG4 with reduced effector function) failed^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Lecanemab and donanemab clear plaques more rapidly/robustly than earlier antibodies

docs.title: Disease Modification
docs.text: Amyloid removal produces: - Cognitive benefit: ~30% slowing over 18 months^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Tau slowing: Reduced tau pathology progression (measured by tau-PET and p-tau biomarkers)^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Reduced neuroinflammation: Attenuated GFAP and other inflammatory markers^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Dose-dependent effects: Correlation between magnitude of amyloid removal and downstream benefits^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Modest slowing: 30% benefit vs robust amyloid clearance^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • Co-pathologies persist: Tau, neuroinflammation, lipid dyshomeostasis become semi-autonomous after amyloid seeding^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • Earlier intervention better: TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 stratified by tau-PET showed greater benefit with less advanced disease^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Validated Hypothesis
docs.text: After decades of failed anti-amyloid trials, 2023 marked a paradigm shift: - CLARITY-AD and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 validated that amyloid removal can slow AD^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md] - Supports amyloid as causative driver of downstream pathologies^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Approved Therapies
docs.text:
• Lecanemab: Anti-Aβ protofibril antibody; approved for early AD
  • Donanemab: Anti-pE3-Aβ antibody; approved for early AD

docs.title: Future Directions
docs.text:
• Complementary therapies targeting tau and neuroinflammation needed^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • CAR-based therapies (CAR macrophages, CAR-T cells, CAR astrocytes) targeting amyloid in preclinical development^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]
  • Preclinical trials testing prevention in asymptomatic at-risk individuals (AHEAD 3-45, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3)^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Aβ is the earliest detectable pathology in AD and a validated therapeutic target. Understanding its structural heterogeneity and pathogenic species enables more targeted diagnostics and therapeutics. The clinical success of anti-Aβ antibodies represents the first disease-modifying treatments for AD, transforming the therapeutic landscape from symptomatic management to genuine disease modification.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
1. Species specificity: Is therapeutic effect due to targeting specific Aβ species (protofibrils vs pE3-Aβ) or the speed/magnitude of clearance?^[raw/articles/recent-advances-alzheimers-disease-cell-review-2026.md]

  2. Structural consequences: What are the biological pathways activated by different Aβ conformations?

  3. Optimal timing: How early must intervention begin to prevent cognitive decline?

  4. Combination therapies: What complementary approaches (anti-tau, anti-inflammatory, lipid modulation) will provide additive/synergistic benefits?

  5. Prevention: Can anti-amyloid therapies prevent AD in asymptomatic at-risk individuals?

  • neuroinflammation: Aβ clearance attenuates neuroinflammation; microglial activation required for therapeutic effect

  • : Anti-Aβ antibodies first to show clinical benefit
  • : Amyloid PET, CSF Aβ42/40, plasma Aβ for detection and monitoring

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text: Myth Reality Aβ plaques are the sole cause of AD Aβ is initial trigger but co-pathologies (tau, inflammation, lipid dysregulation) drive cognitive decline Any anti-Aβ antibody will work Pathogenic species matter: protofibrils and pE3-Aβ are therapeutic targets, monomers are not Amyloid removal should halt disease Amyloid removal slows but doesn't stop progression due to semi-autonomous co-pathologies Synthetic fibrils model human disease Brain-derived filaments have different structures; synthetic fibrils may not accurately model disease Cognitive decline correlates with amyloid burden Cognitive decline correlates more strongly with tau pathology; amyloid is upstream trigger
