docs.text:
00:00 Today we’re going to talk about the darker aspects of war.

00:03 Yes, war is dark enough in itself, but as you’ll know from some of our other shows

00:07 many despicable things happen in war behind what we might call closed doors.

00:12 We only need to look at the Nazi doctor, Josef Mengele, who conducted experiments on people

00:18 that make your stomach churn.

00:20 We might also look at the Nazi ‘Death Marches”, the massacres, the genocides, the torture

00:24 of prisoners and prisoners literally being worked to death.

00:28 These things all happened during the Second World War, as did biological warfare and the

00:33 testing of deadly agents on those captured by certain militaries.

00:36 But today we’ll focus on just one matter of total depravity during that war, in this

00:41 episode of the Infographics Show, The Horror of Unit 731.

00:45 Unit 731 was the brainchild of the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.

00:50 It was a biological and chemical warfare research unit that conducted experiments on prisoners

00:55 with the aim of developing deadly weapons.

00:57 It’s written that at its base in China – remember the Japanese were at war with China – around

01:02 3,000 men, women, and children were tested on.

01:05 Most of these we are told were Chinese, but some of them were from the Allied Nations,

01:10 the Soviet Union, Korea and Mongolia.

01:12 The unit lasted until the end of the war in 1945 and it’s written that it had ample

01:17 funding from the Japanese government.

01:19 Ok, so this unit was developing dastardly weapons and it needed to test those weapons

01:23 on people first.

01:25 But other tests were also done, related to trying to understand what the human body could

01:29 endure.

01:30 That way the Japanese military might better understand what its own soldiers could go

01:34 through.

01:35 The Cold One of the things many soldiers had to put

01:37 up with during the war was cold, and cold did kill a lot of people.

01:42 At Unit 731 they wanted to understand just how cold someone could get and still survive.

01:47 The website Unit731.org tells us, “Some human test subjects were taken outside during

01:53 the harsh winter until their limbs froze off for the doctors to experiment how best to

01:57 treat frostbite.”

01:59 The New York Times, which had testimonies from people who had seen the horrors of this

02:02 unit, wrote that these people would be taken outside and guards would throw water on them

02:07 until they saw the victim had frostbite.

02:09 Sometimes, wrote the newspaper, the guard would hit the arm of the prisoner with a stick

02:13 and if he heard something like a wood-against-wood sound he knew the arm was totally frozen.

02:18 What happened next is the doctors would use various methods to try and unfreeze the arm

02:22 or other body part.

02:24 Sometimes the prisoner would be left alone to unfreeze, sometimes warm water would be

02:28 thrown on him or her and sometimes much warmer water.

02:32 The Japanese doctors, according to The Times, concluded that water over 100 degrees fahrenheit

02:36 but never more than 122 degrees fahrenheit worked the best.

02:41 Vivisection The Japanese military also wanted to know

02:43 how best to treat disease and injuries, but we are told that to do this they would often

02:48 use live prisoners to operate on.

02:50 It’s said that some of these prisoners would be deliberately given a disease, and then

02:54 the doctors would open up the body of the patient without any kind of anesthesia.

02:57 They wanted to look at the effects of the disease before the body began decomposing,

03:01 and that’s why they kept the subjects alive.

03:05 These people were called marutas, or logs.

03:07 The New York Times, with testimony from a former surgeon, said they just wanted to know

03:11 what had happened inside.

03:13 That man told the Times, “I cut him open from the chest to the stomach, and he screamed

03:18 terribly, and his face was all twisted in agony.

03:20 He made this unimaginable sound, he was screaming so horribly.

03:24 But then finally he stopped.

03:26 This was all in a day's work for the surgeons, but it really left an impression on me because

03:30 it was my first time.”

03:32 Testing Pathogens One of the major experiments at Unit 731 was

03:36 to test how certain pathogens, including cholera or anthrax, would affect a number of people

03:42 if they were exposed to the pathogens.

03:43 They didn’t just do this inside the camp, but also did what they called field testing.

03:48 This was done by dropping the pathogens on small communities in China.

03:52 They wanted to see if they could cause an outbreak of disease.

03:55 We are told some of these experiments were successful, so the Japanese then had the idea

03:59 to carry these pathogens to the United States in what were called balloon bombs.

04:03 It’s written that the Japanese did send about 200 balloons to the U.S. but these failed

04:08 for the most part, only leading to the death of seven people.

04:11 They also had a plan to drop plague-infected fleas on San Diego by using Kamikaze pilots.

04:18 Testing Weapons The Japanese also wanted to test weapons that

04:21 they could use on the battlefield, and this included regular weapons but also toxic gases.

04:26 To do this prisoners would be taken out to a field and tied to a spot with a stake.

04:30 The soldiers would then start testing, which sometimes just meant shooting guns at the

04:34 target, and other times throwing grenades at certain distances to see how effective

04:38 they were.

04:39 The bodies of the victims would then be analyzed so the Japanese knew exactly what damage their

04:44 weapons could do.

04:45 We are told that in one experiment gas was fired at the tied-up prisoners, but the wind

04:49 changed direction and it sent the Japanese soldiers running.

04:53 It’s also said that the soldiers would occasionally test their flamethrowers on the prisoners.

04:57 The pressure chamber and spinning While Japanese people who had worked in the

05:01 camp later recalled how many parts of prisoners could be seen in jars all over the camp, it’s

05:06 not always known how those people died.

05:08 Perhaps one of the worst deaths was the pressure chamber.

05:10 We are told that prisoners would be placed inside a pressure chamber, sometimes alongside

05:14 another prisoner, and the pressure would be turned up until basically the prisoners’

05:19 eyes popped and they eventually died.

05:21 If that wasn’t horrific enough, other prisoners would be literally spun to death so that the

05:26 military could test centrifugal forces.

05:28 Operations The Japanese also wanted to have better surgeons,

05:32 and those surgeons needed subjects to work on.

05:34 One report found tells us how one subject was given an appendectomy.

05:38 After that, his arm was removed and after that he received a tracheotomy.

05:42 This all took about 90 minutes and when the doctors were done, they just killed that patient.

05:47 The man who did these surgeries was at the time a student doctor.

05:50 He told the media that he’d had no idea what to expect when he was told he was going

05:54 to China to practice surgeries.

05:57 Spreading syphilis This is the testimony from a worker at Unit

06:00 731: “Infection of venereal disease by injection was abandoned, and the researchers started

06:06 forcing the prisoners into sexual acts with each other.”

06:09 It’s said that if the pair refused, they would be shot.

06:11 At other times children were infected with the disease.

06:14 The reason this happened was so those infected prisoners could be vivisected at various stages

06:18 of the disease and the doctors at the camp could better understand how it affected a

06:23 person’s organs during that stage of infection.

06:26 Forced pregnancy It’s said that female prisoners would be

06:29 made pregnant by force so that the doctors could understand if disease was passed to

06:33 the child.

06:34 They also wanted to know what damage a disease may have caused to the woman’s reproductive

06:38 organs during pregnancy.

06:39 It’s said the guards would just take women and do this, even to those already injured

06:44 from other experiments.

06:45 While many children were thought to have been born on the camp, it’s said that none survived.

06:50 One former soldier said this sometime later, “Of course there were experiments on children.

06:54 But probably their fathers were spies.”

06:57 For a long time this unit was not talked about, but The Guardian reported in 2018 that Japan

07:02 released lots of information from its national archives relating to Unit 731.

07:07 Prior to this, much of what we knew was only based on testimonies.

07:10 No one has denied what we have talked about today did not happen, but there are more reports

07:15 that tell us smaller experiments also happened.

07:18 These included people being exposed to dangerous levels of radiation, being injected with the

07:22 blood from animals, being injected with sea water and also being burned alive.

07:27 It’s said during the war the Americans knew about the camp and after they granted immunity

07:32 to the physicians of Unit 731 if they shared all their findings with the U.S. military

07:36 as some of those findings might be useful and the U.S. didn’t want the Soviets getting

07:40 hold of the research.

07:42 We will leave you with a comment made by a former Unit 731 worker when he was contacted

07:47 some years later.

07:48 “I don't want to think about Unit 731.

07:50 Fifty years have passed since the war.

07:52 Please let me remain silent.”

07:54 Do you think anything like this could happen again?

07:57 How do you think people could do to this other human beings?

08:00 Tell us in the comments.

08:01 Also, be sure to check out our other video Could You Survive the Stanford Prison Experiment.

08:05 Thanks for watching, and as always, don’t forget to like, share and subscribe.

08:09 See you next time.

00:00 8 am. April 2, 1912. The magisterial ship the  Titanic leaves the Belfast dock for sea trials.

00:06 Thousands of people have come to watch,

00:08 waving their handkerchiefs in the  air and shouting “Rule Britannia”.

00:12 Some of them chase the ship down the  slipway as she slowly moves away.

00:15 Not one of them could ever expect  that such a behemoth of a vessel

00:19 would end up at the bottom of the icy-cold ocean,  dragging countless people to the depths with it.

00:24 April 10, 1912. On a cold morning, Captain  Edward John Smith arrives at the Southampton dock

00:30 where his crew has been sleeping  on the Titanic through the night.

00:33 Smith is a confident man, and proud of  British shipbuilding expertise. Prior to

00:37 his heading the Titanic he’d told a reporter: “Whatever happens, there will be time enough

00:41 before the vessel sinks to save the life of  every person on board. I will go a bit further.

00:45 I will say that I cannot imagine any condition  that would cause the vessel to founder.”

00:49 Oh, how wrong could he be! We’ll talk  a lot about this guy as things go on.

00:53 Later in the morning, Fifth Officer Harold  Lowe and Sixth Officer James Moody are there

00:58 to supervise a lifeboat drill, unfortunately,  the only one that would happen on the Titanic.

01:02 As midday approaches, the passengers arrive:  rich, poor, and something in between. The ship

01:07 can take 2,453 passengers: 833 in first class,  614 in second class, and 1,006 in third class,

01:16 but there will only be about 2,200  passengers on board when the thing goes down.

01:20 The wealthy board from one entrance and the poor  at another entrance. Those with meager means are

01:25 the third-class passengers, who on arrival are  checked for an eye disease called trachoma.

01:30 The USA doesn’t want these folks, but only  one person it seems is turned away. Lucky him!

01:35 About a third of third-class, dreaming of a new  life in the US, are not native English speakers.

01:40 Their basic cabins reflect their status,  or class, as the British like to call it.

01:44 These are people who will suffer the worst,  screaming in their native tongues as they slide

01:48 down the deck of a ship turning upwards towards  the sky. Some are Bulgarian, Syrian, Italian,

01:54 Swedish, and Russian; some are even Chinese,  even though the Chinese Exclusion Act in the US

01:59 means Chinese laborers aren’t  welcome in the country.

02:02 The first-class passengers enter their  beautiful cabins. These are the bankers,

02:06 businessmen, military leaders, socialites,  athletes, American millionaires,

02:10 and the ever-snooty British aristocracy.

02:12 This is the who’s who of wealthy society,

02:14 and many have arrived with personal  nurses, valets, chefs, and chauffeurs.

02:18 On the ship, they’ll enjoy Turkish  baths, a gymnasium, a squash court,

02:22 a saltwater swimming pool, and even first-class  kennels for their beloved pooches. For their trip,

02:27 and ultimately their death, some of them have  paid around 90,000 bucks in today’s money.

02:32 The second-class passengers: professionals,  academics, religious men, and tourists,

02:37 don’t quite get such luxuries,  but their cabins aren’t too bad.

02:40 It goes without saying that all three classes  will not dine together. They are separated,

02:43 and will only really come together when they are  faced with the matter of life or death. Today,

02:48 these third-class folks will eat rabbit pie,  potatoes, bread and butter, and some rhubarb

02:52 and ginger jam for dessert. The first-class  passengers will devour a 13-course meal,

02:57 including foie gras, peaches in chartreuse  jelly, and a helping of Waldorf pudding.

03:02 It’s early evening on April 10 when  the ship leaves Cherbourg in France

03:06 and heads to Queenstown, Ireland. Some of the  working-class kids are playing on the baggage

03:10 cranes while their parents play cards in the  common room. Life isn’t bad at all on this ship,

03:14 say some of the guys while smoking in  the smoking room - no women allowed!

03:18 As night falls, the upper classes are  already light-headed on champagne,

03:22 talking of their business ventures and mansion  renovations as semi-royal Brits whisper together

03:27 about how vulgar in style and speech one certain  fabulously wealthy American industrialist is.

03:32 They can at least be assured that none of them  will bump into another class, with grilles all

03:36 over the ship that separates the rich and poor. Midday, April 11, and the ship finally arrives

03:42 in Ireland. Many of the wealthy passengers have  just woken up with sore heads, staring down at

03:47 Norwegian salmon and poached eggs. The poor  for the most part have been up since sunrise.

03:51 About 2 pm more passengers board, and the Titanic  is off again. It’s about to get very cold.

03:57 As the ship heads West over the Atlantic,  the captain looks out into the distance.

04:00 The weather is good. The passengers are all  safely on board. So far, he hasn’t given much

04:05 time to the fact that among his crew only about 5  percent are able seamen. Most of the others have

04:10 regular day jobs such as firemen, and little  do they know about the many perils of sailing.

04:15 On April 12, while merriment is being  had by many on board, the morning is

04:19 a wonderful thing to see. The skies are clear,  and the Atlantic is uncharacteristically calm.

04:24 During the afternoon, two young working-class  kids scream for joy as they play hide and seek,

04:29 while America’s first multi-millionaire, the real  estate tycoon and opium smuggler John Jacob Astor,

04:34 talks with the Titanic’s  architect, Thomas Andrews.

04:38 “Is it sinkable,” asks Astor with a smile  on his face. This man is so rich, richer in

04:43 relative terms than any person today, he probably  thinks he’s invincible. Andrews returns the smile,

04:48 answering, “This ship even the great  Poseidon couldn’t sink.” Both men laugh out

04:53 loud as American silent film actress Dorothy  Gibson walks over to see what’s so amusing.

04:58 Both of these men will soon be dead. Gibson  will survive. Women and children first,

05:02 that’s how things will go, although some  men will try their luck. But for now,

05:06 all is perfect, and for two days, life  aboard the Titanic couldn’t be any better.

05:10 As the evening of April 13 turns into the night  and the band plays under a blanket of stars,

05:15 the conditions couldn’t be any better. About  9.30 pm, Captain Smith retires to his cabin,

05:20 his job done for the day. He’s not  aware that the Titanic is about to

05:24 sail under an arctic high-pressure system. In the morning things are not so fine and

05:28 dandy. Around 9 am, senior wireless operator  Jack Phillips is informed by other vessels

05:33 that to the West there are icebergs. The liner  named the Carolina tells him to watch out for

05:37 the hard-to-see Growlers, smaller icebergs  that can still pose a danger to a large ship.

05:42 At 10 am Captain Smith tells his men they  needn’t bother with the lifeboat drill,

05:46 even though he’s been told about  those floating fortresses of ice.

05:49 What this means is his crew, a mostly amateur  crew, does not know much about evacuations.

05:54 We will never know why Smith does this. At midday, the steamship Baltic informs

05:59 the Titanic that larger icebergs wait where  it is heading (42°N, 51° 31′ W). Smith passes

06:02 on the message to the chairman and managing  director of the White Star Line, Bruce Ismay.

06:06 It’s this man that is behind the building of the  Titanic and other huge ocean liners. He is also

06:11 the person that decided such ships needed much  fewer lifeboats than was necessary in times of

06:16 great danger. When the Titanic goes down, he will  make a quick getaway into a lifeboat, even though

06:21 many women and children will still be on board. He’ll be the one who sends a message back

06:25 to the New York office: “Deeply regret advise you

06:28 Titanic sank this morning fifteenth  after collision iceberg, resulting

06:32 serious loss life further particulars later.” One day he’ll open a newspaper and read a poem

06:37 that contains the lines, “To hold your place in  the ghastly face, of death on the sea at night,

06:43 is a seaman's job, but to flee with  the mob, is an owner's noble right.”

06:47 He will survive, but a breakdown will ruin  him, with opiates and booze turning him into

06:52 what his family calls a living “corpse.” But on that afternoon on the 14th when

06:56 he is told about the icebergs, he  doesn’t give it too much thought.

06:59 As the hours pass, though, the passengers,  rich and poor, start putting on extra clothes.

07:03 It’s freezing out there. About this time, Smith  orders his crew to take a different direction.

07:08 In the late afternoon, the Titanic gets a  message from the German ship SS Amerika,

07:12 which is just a bit to the south of the Titanic.  Radio operators on the Amerika tell the radio

07:17 operators on the Titanic that it has just “passed  two large icebergs.” This is now getting serious,

07:22 but Smith doesn’t get this particular message. As the evening falls, the weather is now

07:27 bitterly cold. The SS Californian tells  the Titanic that it has just seen three

07:31 large icebergs close to where the Titanic  might be heading. Later, at about 9.30 pm,

07:35 the steamer Mesaba tells the Titanic’s operators  that it has just seen “much heavy pack ice and

07:40 great number of large icebergs. Also field ice.” Jack Philips hears these warnings loud and clear,

07:46 but he never relays them to Smith and the others  in charge. This is a major mistake, a fatal

07:51 mistake, but it has to be said that the day before  the radio equipment had been broken and that meant

07:56 Smith had a deluge of messages from passengers  that he still needed to send. Some of the VIPs

08:01 on that ship have serious business to attend to. At 10.30 pm that night Philips receives another

08:06 message from Cyril Evans of SS Californian.  He is informed that the Californian has had

08:11 to halt for the night in an ice field. “Say,  old man, we are stopped and surrounded by ice,”

08:16 says Evens. It is just too dangerous to go on. Smith replies to the message with the words,

08:21 “Shut up! Shut up! I'm working Cape Race.”  Newfoundland’s Cape Race is the relay station for

08:25 the radio messages. About this time there are some  changes on the Titanic’s bridge. First Officer

08:31 William Murdoch tells Second Officer Charles  Lightoller that he’ll now take over the watch.

08:36 Lightoller will become the man that makes  sure, for the most part at least, that the

08:40 order of women and children first is adhered to.  He’ll be the most senior officer to survive the

08:44 disaster and even become a hero of the evacuation  of Dunkirk in WW2. Just before his shift is over,

08:50 he tells the lookouts to “keep a sharp look-out  for ice, particularly small ice and growlers.”

08:56 Once Murdoch is on watch, his nerves  become jangled. Danger is out there

09:00 in the ocean, but it is a danger  that seems cloaked in invisibility.

09:03 As he looks into the distance at around 11 pm,  the majority of the passengers have retired to

09:07 their cabins without an inkling of the  precarious position their lives are in.

09:11 Two lookouts named Frederick Fleet and Reginald  Lee are now in the Titanic's crow's nest. They

09:16 struggle to see any icebergs, mainly because of  the fact that the sea is so calm, which means the

09:20 water isn’t hitting the ice and making a splash.  It doesn’t help matters that they don’t have any

09:25 binoculars. The guy with the locker key where  they’re kept has them, and that’s no use now.

09:30 They are alone as the Californian now  turns off its radio. At around 11.30,

09:35 lookout Fleet rings the bell. He’s just seen an  iceberg and the Titanic is heading right into it.

09:40 Fleet asks the bridge, “Is there anyone there?”  He then hears the reply, “Yes, what do you see?”

09:44 To which he responds, “Iceberg, right ahead!” Murdoch gives the order for the ship to

09:48 “hard-a-starboard” and reverses the engines,  as well as ordering that all the supposedly

09:54 air-tight doors to the compartments are locked. A few minutes later, at 11.40, the Titanic scrapes

09:59 past the giant iceberg, making a frightening noise  as it does so. This is one great chunk of ice.

10:05 The Titanic has before been moving at a fairly  fast speed of 22 knots (41 km/h; 25 mph), so

10:09 despite the order to reverse the engines,  it can’t slow down fast enough to move out

10:13 of the way of the iceberg. Captain Smith had  promised a swift journey to his passengers, and

10:16 he wasn’t about to disappoint them. Such haste,  we now know, was one reason for the disaster.

10:22 That order to hard-a-starboard, which takes  some doing, has caused technical problems

10:27 that mean the rudder isn’t functioning right.  If Murdoch had instead ordered the ship to

10:31 maintain its speed and turn, and not reverse the  engines, it may have actually missed the berg.

10:36 The ship has scraped along that ice for about  seven seconds, and on doing so, chunks of ice

10:40 have even fallen onto the deck. Its engines have  now stopped and it's facing north while drifting

10:45 south. There is an eerie silence on board and  among some of the men a feeling of great anxiety.

10:50 They have every right to feel anxious because  a large rip has been made in the hull. The hole

10:55 below the water is around 12 square feet (1.1 m2),  although the tear stretches for around 300 feet.

11:01 Why a hole has been torn through such a tough  ship will be debated for many years to come.

11:05 Ships just as strong will later  get thorough whackings and survive,

11:09 but that’s the future and we  are not speculating today.

11:12 Many of the passengers feel a thud as the ship  makes contact with the iceberg, more so those

11:16 on the lower decks. The Titanic is taking on lots  of water, something not evident to many just yet.

11:22 Seven tons a second are flooding the ship,  which is much faster than it can be pumped out.

11:26 By about 11.50, so much water has entered the ship  that the front part has risen. In a boiler room,

11:32 all hell is breaking loose. Second engineer J.  H. Hesketh and leading stoker Frederick Barrett

11:38 are both blasted by icy water and  get out of the room just in time.

11:41 They are now aware, as are the other engineers  that know what’s going on, that if the freezing

11:46 cold water hits the hot steam an explosion could  blow them to pieces, although most of them are

11:50 soon to die anyway. Some of them have been ordered  to vent the steam so as to stop an explosion.

11:55 All of them are now up to their waists in water. The main problem is what’s happening on the 16

12:00 lower decks, not up top where not many people  have even batted an eyelid over the crash.

12:05 The third-class passengers are down below, most  of them on F Deck, with some on E Deck, along

12:10 with the second-class passengers. Deck D contains  a number of rooms, including the first-class

12:15 dining saloon. Deck C is home to a library and  lounge for second-class folks as well as an

12:20 all-male smoking room for third-class passengers. It isn’t until you get to Deck B that you have the

12:25 first-class cabins and suites as well as the à  la carte restaurant, Café Parisien. Deck A is

12:31 for the first-class promenade and among other  things, the all-male first-class smoking room.

12:36 So, it’s the poorer passengers that really  hear that thud, even though they’re already

12:40 accustomed to the loud noises issuing from the  engines. Even if they are scared and want to

12:44 go up to a higher deck, they aren’t able to  since they’re locked out of those places.

12:48 It’s now midnight and Captain Smith is aware that  the compartments are filling with water. He’s also

12:52 aware that the Titanic is not designed to float  with water-filled compartments, and right now

12:57 water is seeping into them at an alarming rate.  Once one is filled, the next one starts to fill,

13:02 with experts later saying the effect was  like that of filling a tray of ice cubes.

13:06 He orders the lifeboats to be prepared for  an evacuation, but the fact is there are only

13:10 enough of them for about half the crew and  passengers. You already know why. Meanwhile,

13:15 the radio operators are busy putting out  CQD calls. The D part stands for distress.

13:20 The closest ship it seems at first is the  Frankfurt and that’s about 170 nautical

13:24 miles (315 km) away, to the south of the  Titanic. The Titanic's sister ship the Olympic

13:28 also gets the message, but it is way off in the  distance. The Titanic is on its own for now.

13:33 Still not long after midnight, Smith  and the ship’s builder, Thomas Andrews,

13:37 who we’ve mentioned already, go down  below as the ship starts to list.

13:40 There they find the holds filled with water, as  is the squash court, and while men are busy trying

13:45 to pump the water out, they just can’t get ahead. The first-class women and children are now on the

13:50 deck waiting for the lifeboats, with many of them  in tears, clutching onto each other. It’s at this

13:54 point when many of the passengers know this  ship is in trouble, although they don’t know

13:58 about the lifeboat shortage and many of them  still don’t think there is a major problem.

14:03 Some are very reluctant to get into a lifeboat.  The Titanic, they assume, just won’t sink.

14:08 The good news, at least for the operators and  captains, is that at around 12.20 am a ship not

14:13 too far away gets the distress call and replies.  That ship, the Carpathia, hears the words,

14:18 “Come at once. We have struck a berg. It's a CQD,  old man.” The coordinates are given as 41°46’ N

14:25 50°14’ W. The Carpathia changes course, but it’s  still around 58 nautical miles (107 km) away.

14:31 It will be a matter of hours until  it can get close to the Titanic.

14:34 Among the chaos that has now descended on the  ship, the musicians are playing on the deck in an

14:39 attempt to keep people calm. Before ALL of these  men die, they play mostly popular ragtime tunes,

14:44 and later may just have time to  fit in a version of the hymn,

14:47 “Nearer, My God, To Thee.” If this  actually happens is up for debate,

14:51 but it makes a nice story if it's true. It is about 12.30 when five compartments

14:55 are totally filled with water, about 13,700  tons of the stuff, which means the Titanic

15:00 will not stay afloat much longer. Maybe it’s  got two hours before it is completely submerged.

15:04 For now, it is only at about a four-degree angle  and for the while at least it won’t get much

15:08 worse, and this gives the crew and the passengers  a false sense of security. Maybe she won’t totally

15:13 sink, some of them think, but they’re very wrong.  Pity, because some of them have refused to go

15:18 on the lifeboats, which is another reason why most  of the boats left with way too few people on them.

15:23 It’s around this time that some of the crew have  another reason to be hopeful. They see a ship in

15:27 the distance, so fire off a bunch of rockets.  That ship is very likely a Norwegian fishing

15:32 vessel doing a spot of illegal hunting. The  Californian does actually see those rockets, but

15:37 it is still some 20 nautical miles (37 km) away. It’s 12.45 and Smith is now loading the first

15:42 lifeboats, the regular ones that can take  65 people on board. Even though the ship

15:46 already doesn’t have enough boats, Smith keeps  letting them go well under capacity. The first

15:51 floats away with only 27 people on it. He is arguably to blame for many deaths,

15:56 yet for many years he will be a hero. He never  gives an abandon ship order, and he doesn’t even

16:01 do a proper evacuation, not to mention the fact  that he wasn’t taking those iceberg warnings

16:05 seriously enough. He even gets the deck wrong when  he first orders people to get into the lifeboats.

16:10 As the gravity of what is going to  happen hits him, Smith becomes almost

16:13 paralyzed with shock and fear. He isn’t  in control at all and hasn’t even told the

16:18 crew the truth about the lifeboat situation. At 12.55, the second lifeboat hits the water,

16:23 and as it does, two cowardly men jump down  into it, inuring some of the women. The

16:27 next one to go has on it the passenger  Molly Brown, a rich American socialite.

16:32 She will also become famous in time to come,  mainly because she wanted to go back and pick

16:36 up people in the water. Robert Hichens, who was  steering the Titanic when it hit the iceberg,

16:40 will also be in that lifeboat and he will  tell Brown that there is no point going

16:44 back for “stiff” bodies, and anyway, it is too  risky as those left alive might swamp the boat.

16:50 He’ll deny this later but will admit  that he was concerned that the suction

16:53 of the sinking Titanic might pull  down the lifeboat. By all accounts,

16:57 Brown threatened to throw him in the water,  but they never went back to find survivors.

17:01 At 1 am, a smaller lifeboat, a wooden cutter,  hits the water, filled with some wealthy women

17:06 and children. Controversially, the rich Scottish  landowner, the 5th Baronet, Cosmo Duff-Gordon,

17:11 is also in the boat, along with his wife,  Lady Duff Gordon, a famous fashion designer.

17:16 Other rich men are in that boat,

17:17 as is a lookout who’s been put in charge  named George Thomas Macdonald Symons.

17:22 Five other crew are also on the boat.  It can hold 40 people but only takes 12.

17:26 Later, it will be suggested that Cosmo  Duff-Gordon paid a bribe to get away and

17:30 not pick up any struggling people in the water,  but whether that happened is also debatable.

17:35 As that boat floats away, one of the crew  says he wants to go back and help the others,

17:38 but the women protest. Once they are in the  distance, Lady Duff Gordon surprises one of

17:42 the crew when she looks at another wealthy woman  and states, “There is your beautiful nightdress

17:47 gone.” This is going to cause quite the stink  within the British public once it gets out.

17:52 On the Titanic, there is a major concern  when some of the crew see that on Deck E

17:56 the Grand Staircase is now covered  in water. It’s just past 1.

18:00 At around the same time, another waste of  life occurs when a lifeboat is lowered with

18:04 just 28 people on it. One of them is the  first-class passenger Lucy Noël Martha,

18:08 countess of Rothes, as well as Ida Straus, the  wife of Macy’s department store owner, Isidor.

18:14 She lets go of his hand and gets in the  boat, motioning him to go with them.

18:18 He likely can if he tries, but he tells  her “Women and children first darling”.

18:22 She looks at him and replies, “We have lived  together for many years. Where you go, I go.”

18:26 She gets right back out. The two of them will go  down together on the ship in each other’s arms.

18:31 The last sighting of them is hugging on the deck. You might be wondering where all the third-class

18:35 passengers are. It’s true that there are  grills that prevent them from getting to

18:39 other parts of the ship, but they aren’t locked  in with the sinking ship out of sheer brutality.

18:43 They are in fact behind bars, but that’s only  because they’ve been that way from the start of

18:47 the journey due to US immigration laws regarding  immigrants and certain infectious diseases.

18:52 It’s still brutal, cruel, inhumane, and more  so when you hear that there are no lifeboats

18:57 on the third-class sections of the ship. Many of these passengers are now running

19:00 through the maze of corridors  trying to find a safer place,

19:03 and fortunately, the staircases lead some of them  to the third and second-class promenade where

19:08 there are lifeboats. Nonetheless, some of them  are faced with iron grills and locks, at least

19:12 until the orders are given to open the gates. One of them is Carl Jansson. He goes back to

19:17 his room to gather what belongings he has,  only to be hit by the great force of water.

19:21 He at least gets his watch but returns to  the deck to people stricken with terror.

19:25 He survives, but many of those people don’t. Some of them are understandably unwilling to

19:29 leave all their worldly possessions behind.  Remember they are going to the US to start a

19:33 new life. But, many of them have also been trapped  by those gates and they will die because of it.

19:38 Margaret Murphy sees this with her  own eyes. She will later testify:

19:42 “The Titanic's sailors fastened the doors and  companionways leading up from the third-class

19:46 section. A crowd of men was trying to get up  to a higher deck and were fighting the sailors;

19:51 all striking and scuffling and swearing. Women  and some children were there praying and crying.

19:56 Then the sailors fastened down the hatchways  leading to the third-class section.

20:00 They said they wanted to keep the air down there  so the vessel could stay up longer. It meant all

20:04 hope was gone for those still down there.” Even though there is a women and children

20:08 first policy for the evacuation, 108  women will die from a possible 412.

20:13 56 kids will die from a possible 112. Of 1680 men,  1357 will die. But get this, only four women who

20:22 have bought first-class tickets will die, and  only one wealthy child will die. First-class

20:27 men don’t have it so easy, either, with 105 going  to meet Davy Jones' Locker from 171 in that class.

20:34 On the other hand, of the 179 women in  third-class, 91 will bite the dust. 391 men in

20:40 third-class from 450 will die, and 55 out of 80  kids with those cheap tickets will also perish.

20:46 So yes, while investigations later rule that there  hadn’t been any malice against the ship’s poor,

20:50 the game on the ship had been the same as the  game in life, rigged against them from the start.

20:55 What’s quite touching is when the orders are first  given to let the women and children go first,

20:59 most of the third-class men don’t  try to jump on the boats. In fact,

21:03 reports later stated they stood back and said  goodbye to their families and they took it on

21:07 the chin. A few didn’t, but we’ll get to them. At 1.20 am these men are quite aware that they

21:13 are possibly going to die. It’s at that  time that another lifeboat is lowered,

21:17 this one containing a special passenger. That’s  a nine-year-old girl named Millvina Dean,

21:22 who will die in 2009 at the age of  97, the last of the survivors to go.

21:27 There is a mix of people on this  lifeboat, and with 56 passengers on board,

21:31 it’s at least one that leaves carrying a  substantial number of people. Another one

21:34 of them is the mistress of the super-wealthy  American businessman Benjamin Guggenheim.

21:39 He waves her goodbye and tells his valet to  get dressed in smart clothes. Some of his

21:43 last words are, “We've dressed up in our best  and are prepared to go down like gentlemen.”

21:47 At 1.30, not all the men are so cool-headed.  Several of them try and hustle their way

21:52 into lifeboat 14, which forces Fifth  Officer Harold Lowe to fire his gun

21:55 a few times in the air and shout, “Get  back or I’ll shoot you all like dogs.”

22:00 Just after 1.30, lifeboat 13 is lowered, this one  containing a number of third-class passengers.

22:05 Only as it goes down, lifeboat 15 is  lowered too fast and it drops on 13,

22:10 causing some amount of distress. Thankfully,  a crew member on 13 manages to cut the ropes

22:14 and the boat floats away. It’s around this time  that Philips gets on the radio again and says,

22:19 “Women and children in boats.  Cannot last much longer.”

22:22 At 1.40, there aren’t many lifeboats left to  go. Number 16 drifts away into the darkness,

22:27 followed by Collapsible boat C, containing Mr.  Ismay and mostly women. Lifeboat 11 then leaves.

22:33 The emergency cutter number 2 is ready  to go, but Lightoller is dismayed to

22:37 find it filled with men who he says are not  “British, nor of the English-speaking race”

22:41 and he threatens them with his gun. Women and  children take their place, but it’s lowered with

22:45 just 25 people on it when it can take 40. You might remember the multi-millionaire,

22:50 John Astor. He watches his pregnant wife,  Madeleine, get into lifeboat number 4. She

22:54 pleads with him to follow her, but Lightoller  tells him he won’t be going anywhere. Astor says,

22:59 “We are safer here than in that little boat.” It  leaves with enough space for another 20 people.

23:04 It’s 2 in the morning now and the only  way off the Titanic is on one of the three

23:07 collapsible boats that are left. Things  don’t look good. The ship has tilted so

23:11 much now that its propeller is out of the water. The lights go out, and they are swallowed by the

23:15 darkness. In the distance, the survivors in the  lifeboats begin to cry for those they left behind.

23:20 Now they can hear screams emanating from the ship,  betwixt the groaning of the floundering ship.

23:25 Second Class Passenger Father Thomas Byles has  been on the stern of the Titanic listening to

23:30 people’s final confessions. The band is still  playing. But there’s trouble in the radio room

23:34 when a man tries to steal a life vest. Officer Lightoller now knows it’s do or die,

23:39 so gets on the roof of the officers'  quarters and dives into the freezing water.

23:42 Maybe lady luck has ideas for him, because  after being sucked into a ventilation shaft

23:47 he is pushed back out by hot air. Back on the Titanic,

23:50 the forward funnel has collapsed.

23:52 It crushes many people, including  the founder of the Internalization

23:55 Tennis Federation, Charles Duane Williams.

23:58 The next collapsible can’t even be launched,  being swept off the deck at 2.12 am and taking

24:03 a few people with it. When it lands upside  down in the water, about 30 men cling to it,

24:07 including wireless operator Bride and Officer  Lightoller, who’s had another bit of luck.

24:12 They eventually get picked up by lifeboats 4 and  12, but hundreds are now freezing in the water.

24:17 Collapsible Boat A just about  makes it off the deck at 2.15,

24:20 but is soon swamped with people. First-class  passenger Edith Evans is one of them,

24:25 but she like the others ends up in the water and  dies. To think, she has just given up her place

24:29 in another boat. The only female who goes down  with the Titanic and survives is Rhoda Abbott,

24:34 even though she refuses to leave her  two teenage sons behind. They both die.

24:39 On the deck, Captain Smith  tells those that are left,

24:41 “It’s every man for himself.” He’s seen one last  time on the bridge after that. He either goes down

24:46 with the ship or jumps overboard just before  it goes down. There are differing accounts.

24:50 The last anyone sees of Thomas Andrews is him  sitting quietly in the first-class smoking room.

24:55 He makes no attempt at all to escape, although  some accounts have him throwing deckchairs into

24:59 the ocean for the passengers that have gone  overboard. Either way, he dies. He might even

25:03 jump overboard with Smith. That’s how hectic  things are. People are seeing different things.

25:08 It’s almost the end now. As the ship tilts steeply,

25:11 people try and cling on to one another, but  a large gush of water pulls them overboard.

25:15 Others are washed down the deck, their bodies  mangled against various parts of the ship.

25:19 At 2.18, the ship breaks in two. The bow sinks  into the ocean and at a speed of 30 miles per

25:24 hour (48 kph), it takes about six minutes to  reach the bottom. The stern levels for a while,

25:28 but then violently rises, throwing people all  over the place. Those few that manage to cling

25:32 to something are doing so in vain because the  entire ship is about to plunge into the abyss.

25:37 It is 2.20 when some of the people in  the lifeboats hear the Titanic finally

25:40 being swallowed by the water. There  is one last groan, and that’s it.

25:44 But even worse, because the ship goes down  with so much force that it takes tables,

25:48 chairs and huge chunks of timber and steel down  with it. A lot of the debris comes right back up,

25:54 and does so with some speed, killing the swimmers  on impact. It’s likely they’ll die anyway, with

26:00 −2 °C (28 °F) water being enough to finish most  people off in a few minutes. That’s if the shock

26:05 of being submerged hasn’t already killed them. Many swimmers die between 15 and 30 minutes in the

26:10 water, their bodies going into cardiac arrest.  Only 13 of them are fished out by lifeboats,

26:15 even though if all the boats go back  500 people can be helped. It’s anyone’s

26:19 guess how many folks could be saved, but  that some people needlessly died is true.

26:24 As they float through the water in the  darkness, the survivors hear shouts of anger,

26:28 cries of distress, screams of pain, sounds they  will never forget. One of the survivors will

26:32 later sum up what he hears, saying, it was “a  dismal moaning sound which I won't ever forget;

26:37 it came from those poor people who were  floating around, calling for help. It

26:41 was horrifying, mysterious, supernatural.” At times the lifeboats float past a person.

26:46 Its occupants apologize for not helping  the swimmer, but rather than become upset,

26:49 the swimmer just says, “I understand”  and “good luck and God bless you.”

26:53 But as they float on, they hear one man,  perhaps the last man, shout, “My God!

26:57 My God!” As he freezes his voice loses hope until  all that is left is silence. That’s all there

27:03 is after a while: stiff bodies and silence. But one guy who does survive for a long time

27:08 in the water is the Titanic’s  chief baker, Charles Joughin.

27:11 Prior to the sinking of the Titanic, he  drinks more whiskey than is humanly possible,

27:16 having just turned down the offer to get in  lifeboat 10. Right before he heads for his drink,

27:20 he persuades reluctant women to get in the boats. When he emerges on the deck, most people have

27:24 gone, so he throws a bunch of chairs in  the ocean to use as floatation devices,

27:28 but then he changes his mind. He grabs  hold of something and in his own words,

27:32 goes down with the ship as if it is an elevator. He miraculously treads water for about two

27:37 hours, and maybe because of that booze he just  drank, he doesn’t even feel cold. When there’s

27:42 some daylight, he spots a boat. It’s Lightoller’s  boat, but Lightoller denies him a place. Joughin

27:47 holds on to the boat anyway, and then when he  sees another boat, he swims over and gets on that.

27:51 How he survives is anyone’s guess, but later when  asked later he’ll put it down to the whiskey.

27:56 Whatever the case was, he will be known as  the last surviving person on the Titanic.

27:59 He was a tough old boot, that’s for sure. Nonetheless, don’t go thinking booze will stop you

28:04 from getting hypothermia. It actually makes things  worse, so we can’t explain how Joughin survived so

28:09 long when others died in a matter of minutes.  He didn’t panic, which counts for something.

28:14 The first sound heard by the survivors is that of  the approaching Carpathia at around 3.30 am. By 4,

28:20 people are being pulled from the boats, most of  them alive, but more than a few already dead.

28:24 Those with the strength climb onto the ship,  while others are hoisted up with ropes. More

28:28 than 1,500 have died. 706 live to tell the tale. At 8.30 am, the Californian scouts the area

28:34 looking for survivors, but of course there  are none. The others are taken to New York

28:38 City where they’ll arrive on April 18 to  huge crowds and hordes of journalists.

28:42 Some of the surviving crew are interviewed,

28:44 but what really happened on that ship is  something they’re too traumatized to talk about.

28:48 Many questions are later asked, one,  of course, is why so few lifeboats,

28:52 but even with the mass grief and global  outrage, no one is ever really held accountable.

28:56 An act of God is blamed, but we now know  that human error was more to the point.

29:01 Perhaps one of the best artifacts  from the wreckage is a watch that

29:04 was pulled out of the water. That’s because  it stopped when its owner drowned: 2.28 am.

29:09 In 1985, the wreckage was found  12,500 feet (3,800 meters) underwater,

29:13 around 370 nautical miles (690  kilometers) off the coast of Newfoundland.

29:17 The two parts are still now separated  by about 2,000 feet (600 meters).

29:20 It’s the rich and famous whose names we remember,  so we guess the classes on that boat are separated

29:26 even in death, but we remember you third-class  victims: Mrs. Johanna Persdotter Ahlin,

29:31 Mr. Karl Ivar Sven Berglund, Mr. Liudevit Cor,  Miss Kate Conolly, Mr. Lee Bing, and Mr. Fang

29:39 Lang, Mr. Husayn Mahmūd Husayn Ibrāhīm. Ok, we can’t go through all the poor folks

29:44 that died, and to be honest, about 100  of them were buried in unmarked graves.

29:48 But you get the picture. Many of them were  immediately forgotten, while the media and

29:52 public mourned for just a few known names. At  least the fish understood those dead people were

29:56 all the same in the bigger scheme of things. Now you need to watch a video about an equally

30:00 horrific tragedy, “Creepy Reason Nobody Talks  About The Deadliest Ship Disaster In History.”

30:05 Or, have a look at “What If The Earth  Stopped Spinning - Minute By Minute.”

00:00 We’ve been told pandemics are biological  accidents that take years to emerge.

00:05 But what if that’s wrong? New evidence suggests

00:08 something far more unsettling. The next  global killer is already out there,

00:12 waiting and it’s pre-programmed  to hijack your cells right now.

00:15 What if there was never a missing  link in COVID’s origin story?

00:19 Not because of a conspiracy. But because  the virus may never have needed to evolve

00:23 to infect us in the first place. It was born with the master key.

00:27 And if that's true, we're not waiting  for the next pandemic to evolve…

00:31 we're waiting for it to arrive.

00:33 From the very first day of existence, humanity  has had to navigate a biological minefield.

00:37 We knew that there were viruses out there,  invisible to the naked eye. We knew they had

00:42 the potential to wreak havoc inside our bodies  and even bring our lives to an early end.

00:46 We thought we had a certain level of safety. For years - generations, even - public health

00:52 policies, vaccine strategies, and  pandemic response systems were all

00:55 based on a single and important assumption.  That there is a buffer between us and the

01:00 viruses that could potentially wipe us all out. We believed that microbes essentially followed a

01:05 pre-programmed, step-by-step route. First, those viruses would spread

01:08 through that animal population before  eventually jumping into another species,

01:12 like a pangolin, a pig or maybe a civet. And that's where things began to change.

01:17 Inside these new hosts, the  virus would start changing.

01:20 Each infection created new copies. Each new  copy was another chance for a mistake. Another

01:25 mutation. Most went nowhere. But over time,  those mutations could stack up. And eventually,

01:30 the virus might stumble onto the exact  tools it needed to infect humans.

01:35 That’s when we’d need to worry. Once they gained the ability to infect humans,

01:38 they could spread from person to person. As they  moved through the population, they could trigger

01:43 powerful immune responses that make us sick. At  best, that means pain, fever, and discomfort.

01:48 At worst, it can cost lives. Scientists called this buffer the species barrier.

01:53 It was the idea that animal viruses couldn't  simply jump into humans. Before making that leap,

01:58 they were thought to need months, years, or even  decades of evolution inside animal populations.

02:03 It was like a key that still needed to be  filed down before it could fit the unique

02:07 ‘lock’ of the human body. And that mattered.

02:10 It suggested there was distance between us and the  world's most dangerous viruses.The species barrier

02:16 wasn't just a scientific concept. It became a kind of safety net.

02:20 A belief that we’d have a window to  spot a virus spreading through animal

02:23 populations. To track how it was changing  and stop it before it ever reached up.

02:28 But what if that window never existed? What if the virus was already

02:32 loaded and ready to fire? Recent research reveals that the evolutionary

02:36 barrier model may not be anywhere near as concrete  as we thought. Because if viruses need to mutate

02:41 to infect us, then how did the deadliest  outbreaks in history skip this step entirely?

02:47 To understand the implications

02:48 of this biosecurity blind spot, we have  to go back to one of the worst pandemics

02:53 the Earth has ever seen: the Spanish Flu. In just 2 years, it infected roughly a third

02:57 of the world's population and killed tens of  millions of people. It was a uniquely deadly

03:02 strain of H1N1 influenza and it unleashed  chaos on a scale the world had never seen.

03:08 In the decades that followed, scientists  worked to understand exactly how it happened.

03:12 They traced its path and developed  a model for how pandemics spread.

03:16 For nearly a century, we  thought that model was correct.

03:19 The pandemic was portrayed as a slow-motion  disaster. A chain of events that unfolded over

03:24 years, not months. If there had been a warning  window, the tragedy could have been avoided.

03:29 But that narrative was shattered  around the turn of the millennium.

03:32 Scientists exhumed and analyzed the bodies of  Spanish Flu victims from an Inuit community

03:37 in Brevig Mission, Alaska. The bodies had  been perfectly preserved in the permafrost,

03:42 allowing the researchers to extract samples  of the viral RNA. They were then able to

03:46 effectively reconstruct the virus using  modern genomic sequencing techniques.

03:50 That’s when they uncovered the truth. A truth that rewrote the rulebook

03:54 on how viruses operated. It turned out that the 1918

03:58 H1N1 virus hadn’t spent years mutating in pigs  before making the leap into human populations.

04:04 It was believed to have started as an avian  virus, originating in birds. And somewhere

04:08 along the way, it developed something important:  a ‘human-ready’ Hemagglutinin (HA) protein that

04:14 was already capable of binding to human cells. In other words, the virus already had the ‘key’

04:20 it needed to unlock the doors of the human body. At the very moment of spillover as it passed from

04:25 wild bird populations into humans, it didn’t  need to undergo any sort of rapid mutation.

04:30 It didn’t need to multiply to develop the  tools it needed to launch a global pandemic.

04:35 It was a ‘plug and play’  biological weapon found in nature.

04:38 And that completely defied  everything the scientific

04:41 community had believed about this virus. It called into question the idea of a long

04:45 warning window and the so-called  evolutionary barrier itself.

04:49 But every virus is different. They  mutate and move in different ways.

04:52 With that in mind, scientists were  left with one crucial question:

04:56 was 1918 just a bizarre historical fluke?  A once-in-a-lifetime example of a virus

05:01 breaking convention or is nature mass-producing  these ‘plug and play’ weapons as we speak?

05:06 In 2021, a team of researchers

05:08 discovered something that shattered everything  we believed about how viruses operate.

05:12 It was at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic,  caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 strain of coronavirus.

05:18 There were a lot of different theories  about how that particular virus began and

05:22 crossed from animals into humans. Several  studies pointed toward bat populations.

05:27 So, the researchers set out to see if  they could find that ‘missing link’.

05:30 They explored the limestone  caves of Laos in Southeast Asia,

05:33 collecting samples from various bat species  and taking them back to the lab for analysis.

05:38 They uncovered a group of wild bat coronaviruses.  Three in particular - named BANAL-52, BANAL-103,

05:45 and BANAL-236 - stood out due to their  distinctive genomic similarities to SARS-CoV-2.

05:51 Further analysis showed that all 3  of them had a specific spike protein

05:55 that was actually able to attach itself  to the ACE2 receptors of human cells.

06:00 ACE2 receptors act like entry points on the  surface of our cells. Think of them as locks

06:05 and the spike protein are the key viruses use  to open them and gain entry into the body.

06:10 All these viruses possessed the necessary key. But that’s not all.

06:14 Using advanced techniques like binding  measurements and computer simulations,

06:18 researchers found something unexpected. The 3  bat viruses behaved almost identically to the

06:23 original Wuhan strain of SARS-CoV-2.  In some cases, they were even better

06:27 at attaching to human cells, giving the body  almost no chance of preventing an infection.

06:32 One of them, BANAL-236, showed clear evidence  of being able to multiply inside human cells.

06:38 These viruses - found far from  urban centers - were, in some ways,

06:42 better equipped to infect humans than the strain  that was, at the same time, shutting down society.

06:48 Then it got worse. Unlike SARS-CoV-2, none of

06:51 the wild viruses possessed a Furin Cleavage Site,  or FCS. This is a unique molecular structure that

06:57 allows viruses to easily fuse with human cells. At the time, COVID-19 skeptics argued that the

07:03 presence of an FCS was proof that SARS-CoV-2  must have been modified in a laboratory. It’s

07:09 such a rare feature in nature. It was the ‘smoking gun,’

07:13 But the wild viruses proved that Mother Nature  was already producing pre-programmed viral

07:18 strains that could, in theory, bypass the  species barrier. Humans could be infected

07:22 far more easily than expected. All without  the slow, step-by-step evolutionary process

07:27 scientists had long assumed was necessary. And if nature is building these human-optimized

07:32 keys in the middle of the jungle,  what happens when they find a lock?

07:36 Middle East respiratory syndrome-related

07:38 coronavirus, otherwise known as MERS-CoV, is  one of the most lethal pathogens on the planet

07:43 This virus causes a condition called MERS, and  can produce a range of symptoms, from fevers and

07:48 coughs to respiratory difficulties and diarrhea. The first case was identified in 2012 in Saudi

07:53 Arabia. Several thousand more have occurred  since then, with an approximately 35% fatality

07:59 rate. There have been several notable outbreaks,  including one in South Korea in 2015, though most

08:05 cases have been isolated to the Arabian Peninsula. Studies have found that humans are typically

08:10 infected with MERS-CoV via contact with camels. If we follow conventional epidemiological models,

08:16 then the virus found in those camels  should be notably different from the

08:19 one found in the cells of dying human  patients. It should show clear evidence

08:24 of countless mutations that enabled it to pass  from one species to the other. The very changes

08:29 that allowed it to survive in the human body. This would confirm the ‘intermediate host’ theory.

08:34 That’s not what the data shows. When researchers used genomic

08:38 sequencing techniques to map out the MERS-CoV  viruses found in both humans and camels,

08:43 they discovered a disturbing fact:  the two are almost exactly the same.

08:48 To be more precise, they’re 99.9% identical. They’re not distant relatives,

08:54 but biological mirror images. That means that this virus doesn’t

08:57 need any sort of learning or adaptation period  to bridge the gap from one species to the other.

09:02 There isn’t some vast chasm separating the  two, but a tiny, almost imperceptible 0.1% gap.

09:09 The virus can simply cross the species barrier,  using the exact same architecture it relies on

09:14 to infect livestock and other animal populations. It’s a fully functional, completely compatible,

09:20 and capable invader. A microscopic  weapon of mass destruction that is

09:24 more adaptable than we ever thought possible. The implications of this are terrifying from a

09:29 biosecurity standpoint. This discovery suggests  that virologists may have been working on flawed

09:34 information for years. They have been looking  for the wrong warning signs, following unreliable

09:40 models, and allowing society to sleepwalk  its way towards another biological crisis.

09:45 If animal-based viruses like MERS-CoV are  already identical to the human-killing versions,

09:50 then how many more of them are out there,  just waiting to kick off the next pandemic?

09:54 By the early 2020s, we knew that

09:56 there were viruses that could move from animals to  humans far faster than anticipated. Scientists had

10:02 proved that this was the case with the  likes of the Spanish Flu and MERS-CoV.

10:06 But they were still seen by  many as outliers or anomalies.

10:09 Then, a groundbreaking 2024 study arrived.  It showed that these alleged anomalies might

10:14 be part of a larger and deeply worrying trend. The study was carried out by researchers at the

10:19 Bloom Lab at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center,  led by evolutionary biologist Jesse Bloom.

10:24 It was designed to put the evolutionary  barrier hypothesis to the ultimate test.

10:29 They wanted to know whether viruses actually  need time to adapt when they jump into humans,

10:34 or whether they might already be  capable of doing it from the start.

10:37 To do this, the team didn’t just focus  on a single outbreak or viral strain.

10:41 Instead, they analyzed large genomic  datasets to understand how they behave

10:46 at a molecular level. They used a technique  called deep mutational scanning to study

10:51 specific viral proteins in detail. Their  analysis covered a wide range of viruses,

10:56 including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, HIV, and Zika. This allowed them to map out how thousands of

11:03 potential mutations might affect a virus’  ability to evade antibodies and infect cells.

11:08 First, the researchers had to create  so-called ‘pseudoviruses’. These were

11:12 safe versions of real pathogens that were able  to enter cells but unable to replicate. This

11:17 eliminated the multiple risks associated with  working with live, dangerous viral strains.

11:22 They were then able to genetically  engineer the viral proteins to make

11:25 their own mutations, exploring. It was similar  to the ways a viral cell might change or adapt

11:30 to increase its infectivity and ability to survive  in different hosts and environments. The variants

11:35 were then tested and researchers measured how  well they resisted antibodies and how tightly

11:40 they attached themselves to host cells. The data pointed in one direction.

11:44 Some of the deadliest pandemics  in human history had zero

11:47 adaptation time during their initial outbreaks. In other words, when these strains first entered

11:53 the human population, they didn’t immediately need  to evolve to become more effective at infecting us

11:58 or evading the immune system. They didn’t need to.

12:01 They were already capable of doing that. This exposes a truly systemic flaw in global

12:07 health surveillance and security. Scientific communities and virology

12:10 initiatives like the USAID PREDICT program  have believed that we should be looking for

12:15 viruses in the wild that are ‘beginning to  evolve’ human-like traits. The ones that

12:20 could pave the way towards widespread infections. Meanwhile, more ‘generalist’ viruses that are able

12:24 to infect multiple species have historically been  viewed as ‘lower-risk’. That’s because they don’t

12:29 appear to be optimized for human transmission. This research has turned those beliefs upside

12:34 down. It suggests that by the time a virus begins  to evolve human traits it is already too late.

12:40 The pandemic has already started.

12:42 Studies seem to suggest that there could be a  number of viruses out there in the wild today,

12:47 just waiting for human hosts to come  along. The one factor that seemed to be

12:51 working in humanity’s favor was that these viral  strains were confined to places far from human

12:56 populations. They appeared to exist primarily  in jungles, caves, and other remote ecosystems.

13:01 If that was true, then it explained  why global pandemics had seemingly

13:05 been once-in-a-century events. People simply  weren’t coming into contact with these viruses.

13:10 The evolutionary barrier model may have been  shattered, but a new ‘geographic barrier’ seemed

13:15 to have emerged. The actual physical distance  between human populations and infected animals

13:20 helps us to stay relatively safe. That was the theory.

13:24 Researchers made yet another frightening discovery  which sent scientific communities back to the

13:29 drawing board to reassess their understanding of  viral biology. They found that people are actually

13:34 encountering these kinds of viruses. All the time.

13:38 A study was carried out involving almost  700 subjects from rural communities in

13:42 Myanmar. They were screened for signs  of sarbecoviruses: specific sorts of

13:47 coronaviruses that mostly infect bats and  have the potential to cross over into humans.

13:52 The study found that 12.1% of the people possessed  antibodies for these viruses. That meant they had

13:58 been exposed to them at some point in the past. People were significantly more likely to test

14:03 positive if they worked in industries that  involved spending time outdoors or handling

14:07 raw materials. This included activities like  logging, hunting, and harvesting forest products.

14:12 It was an important finding. On average, over 1 in 10 people in these parts of

14:17 the world have been infected by wild viruses. Most  of it appears linked to bats, with some evidence

14:23 also pointing to pangolins. But when you check  official public health records from these same

14:28 areas, you won’t find reports of major outbreaks.  There’s no unexpected spikes in atypical

14:33 infections, no sudden lockdowns or quarantines. But the clues are all there.

14:37 They’re hidden in the blood of these individuals. Those clues are the remnants of the silent ‘test

14:42 fires’ of weapons that haven’t  yet been fully triggered.

14:45 The old explanations of how viruses work have  been well and truly obliterated by this stage.

14:51 Humans aren’t as special as we were led to  believe. Not in the eyes of viruses, in any case.

14:55 We’re just the next step in the chain. Viruses  already have everything they need to infect us,

15:00 and they’re actively doing so, albeit in  places that don’t dominate the headlines.

15:05 If everything we’ve seen so far is accurate,  then humanity’s days must be numbered.

15:10 Evidence suggests that mankind has been

15:12 lucky to survive this far with so many  potentially deadly viruses circulating

15:16 in nature. Fortunately, there’s one thing that  has been working in our favor, this entire time.

15:22 Our last line of defense. A biological safeguard that

15:25 has helped keep humanity alive for generations.  One that has allowed us to survive pandemics

15:30 that killed tens of millions. It’s called the Interferon response.

15:34 And it acts like the body’s built-in firewall. When a human-ready virus enters the body,

15:38 the data suggests it has no trouble binding to  receptors and entering cells. It already carries

15:43 the key it needs to unlock those biological locks.  That’s the easy part. Because the moment it enters

15:49 the body, something else begins. An invisible countdown.

15:52 If the virus doesn’t move fast enough, it won’t  have the freedom it needs to replicate and spread.

15:57 Instead, it’ll be killed out in a matter of hours. This is where the Interferon response comes in.

16:02 Interferons are a group of signaling proteins,  also known as cytokines. They’re produced by

16:08 the body in response to the presence of foreign  microbes, like viruses and bacteria. As their name

16:13 suggests, Interferons are designed to interfere  with these invaders. They slow them down,

16:18 disrupt their replication, and make it  harder for them to take hold in the body.

16:22 They do this in various ways, including  actively degrading viral RNA and alerting

16:27 other cells to defend themselves against the  coming threat. Studies show that the majority

16:31 of wild viruses are entirely neutralized  by this initial cellular counter-attack.

16:36 Even though the viruses have the key to pass the  front door, they soon discover that the house is

16:41 equipped with a state of the art security system. Because for viruses, the real challenge isn’t

16:45 just getting inside the body or even entering  cells. It’s surviving long enough to replicate.

16:51 To multiply fast enough to gain control  before the immune system shuts them down.

16:56 This is the only thing that’s saving us from  a perpetual state of pandemic emergency.

17:01 The warning window depends on the virus itself.  Some viruses mutate quickly, allowing them to

17:05 weaken or evade interferon responses. Others are  stopped earlier. It also depends on the body’s own

17:11 ability to detect the invasion fast enough. To sound the alarm.

17:15 And activate its defenses  before the virus can spread.

17:18 This is why those 1 in 10 people in the rural  villages of Myanmar have those antibodies.

17:22 Yes, their systems were invaded by wild  viruses from bats and other creatures,

17:27 but it didn’t trigger a massive outbreak or  society-halting pandemic. Their bodies were able

17:32 to respond in time and their Interferons  did the job they were designed to do.

17:36 The enemy was effectively eliminated  just inside the castle gates.

17:40 But why is nature building these  human-ready keys in the first place

17:43 if we aren’t the primary target?

17:45 It’s clear humanity has been following  a fundamental misunderstanding

17:49 of viral evolution for generations. We have spent decades believing that viruses

17:53 have to adapt to us because we’re so different and  distinct compared to other animals. Humanity has

17:59 represented the ultimate prize for these microbes,  the pinnacle of their evolutionary pathways.

18:04 The data tells a very different story. It shows that the most successful viral

18:08 strains in history - like the 1918 Spanish Flu  and SARS-CoV-2 COVID-19 - didn’t show any major

18:15 signs of recent human adaptation. These were what virologists

18:18 refer to as ‘generalist’ viruses. They didn’t evolve in the wilderness or mutate

18:23 in dense jungles. They weren’t pre-programmed to  infect and kill humans specifically. They didn’t

18:28 even require years of random mutations  to reach their ‘human-ready’ forms.

18:32 They simply evolved over time to survive in  high-density, multi-species environments.

18:36 They learned to thrive in places where bats,  birds, rodents, primates, and other creatures were

18:41 present. That gives them an enormous advantage. viruses spread more easily when they aren’t

18:46 limited to a single species. These viruses  effectively come with their very own skeleton keys

18:51 that allow them to go almost anywhere they please.  In other words, people aren’t the targets. They’re

18:56 not the end goals or ultimate objectives. They’re just collateral damage.

19:00 This is what makes the next  pandemic an invisible inevitability.

19:04 The hardware is already there. And it’s fully compatible

19:06 with the human operating system. When nature is creating its own biological

19:10 weapons, humanity isn’t sitting on the sidelines.  And when things go wrong, it has consequences.

19:16 Discover the horrifying truth in “Viruses That  Were Actually Lab Leaks”. Or watch this video.
